About this work

Liber Octo Quaestionum ad Maximilianum Caesarem — "A Book of Eight Questions to Emperor Maximilian" — is Trithemius's reply to the eight questions Maximilian put to him at Boppard: on faith and understanding, on the faith necessary for salvation, on the miracles of unbelievers, on witches and harmful magic, and on related matters. Composed in 1508, it is his central statement on witchcraft and the source from which later demonological writers drew heavily. The questions are set out in an enumerated table and answered in sequence, in the blend of scholastic authority and pastoral caution that marks his shorter treatises.

This is the 1515 Oppenheim edition — the first edition of the Octo Quaestionum, printed under imperial privilege. It is the earliest of four witnesses of the text in this corpus (1515, 1534, 1550, 1601). The Latin was re-OCR'd from the page scans and translated by GPT-5.5. A Book of Eight Questions to Emperor Maximilian

Trithemius, Johannes

The Book of Eight Questions addressed to Emperor Maximilian, by Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James at Wurzburg, formerly of Sponheim.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Saint James at Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim: The Book of Eight Questions to Emperor Maximilian.

With the privilege of the imperial majesty: that it not be printed again in his kingdom, empire, and lands, nor copies printed elsewhere sold there, within ten years, under the penalties expressed in the privilege, namely ten marks of pure gold and the loss of all those books, etc.

Epigram of Richard Sbrulius of Friuli.

Who would deny that God is the parent of heaven and earth? No one is so savage as to deny that there is a God. God himself is worshipped everywhere throughout the whole world; he is sought by a different path, yet he is the same. The barbarian worships him as one who orders all things by fixed law; he denies incense to the holy Son and to the Spirit. The Hebrew boasts that he holds the true doctrines, and, with Moses as his leader, thinks himself the people of God. But the people of Christ, who took their name from his name, steadfastly sings that God is triune. Maximilian, greatest, who presides over the empire, continually aids the cause and honor of Christ. He asks, as it is fitting for an august king to ask such things, why the highest God permits there to be so many sects; why he does not present himself equally to all mortals; why he wished many things to lie hidden under hard signs. Father Trithemius sets forth everything to the king in order, that leader and ornament of the hooded flock. Whoever you are who used to doubt concerning the holy faith, read these things; soon you will be a sure pupil of Christ.

To the most serene and most unconquered lord of the world, Emperor Maximilian: Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Peapolitanus, The Book of Eight Questions. In the name of Christ begins the book of the monastery of Benedictbeuern.

I have obeyed your commands, most unconquered Emperor Maximilian, and those eight questions which you formerly proposed to me, when I had been summoned to Your Highness in the castle of Boppard, I have resolved with what brevity I could and set down in this form of a little book.

You wished, however, if I remember correctly, that, so far as possible in their solution, I should follow the path of nature, on account of those who yield less readily to belief. Yet this did not seem possible to me in all matters, because the subject matter of the questions in many places rested upon theological rather than natural principles. For although the Christian religion, among all the sects of mortals, is held to be nearer and more conformable to the laws of nature, nevertheless the principal articles of our faith are not all demonstrable according to the common path of nature. We believe that this was necessarily done so that faith might have a place and firm belief might not lack its own merit.

Therefore, entering upon a middle path of disputation, as far as my powers allowed and by command, I have used partly nature and partly also the testimony of the divine Scriptures. For truly, the things which it is fitting for us to believe are not to be rashly examined by human arguments, since, as Saint Gregory says, faith has no merit when human reason supplies proof for it. Therefore, with fear of God and reverence

of our undefiled Christian religion, I resolved to answer the questions proposed in such a way that I would depart from the definitions of the Roman Church neither in jest nor in earnest. Therefore whatever I have ever written or shall write, I wish all of it to be subject to its determination and judgment.

On Faith and Understanding, the First Question

Question First

The first question of your most serene majesty was this: Why did the all-good God wish to be believed by mortals rather than to be known and understood, namely in that mode of knowledge and understanding by which he is known and understood by the holy angels?

I remember that, when this question was put before your most sacred majesty, I answered as follows. Almighty God, who is without beginning, pure, everlasting, and unchangeable intellect, existing above every position knowable to us and far more perfect than infinite perfections, by his most wise will created from nothing at the beginning two intellects, namely the angelic and the human. The angelic intellect, at the beginning of its creation, was made in act with respect to all knowable things, and it knew all things. The human intellect, however, at first consists in potency with respect to all things, but is ignorant of all things. Yet in the end, through many continual upward actions, it will become like the angelic, knowing both God and all things that pertain to the knowledge of the promised knowledge and understanding.

The angelic and human intellects differ as any two opposites do, namely act and potency, light and darkness, knowledge and ignorance, habit and privation, beginning and end, immobile and mobile, substance and accident, truth and likeness, nature and art, health and infirmity, whole and part. For the angelic intellect is as act, light, knowledge, habit, beginning, immobile, immediate, simple substance, truth, nature, and whole. The human intellect, however, is as potency, darkness, ignorance, privation, end, mobile, mediated, composite, accident, likeness, art, and part.

Hence whatever things belong to the angelic intellect from the beginning, these same things belong to the human intellect at the end, after it has laid aside the burden of flesh; for just as the beginning perfects the angelic intellect by nature, so the end, by art, after many exercises, at last raises the human intellect upward. Therefore between these two intellects there is great inequality from the beginning; nevertheless in the end they are at last made equal, when the human intellect will be as great by art as the angelic had previously been by nature.

Hence it is clear that the angelic intellect, as soon as it was created, from the beginning, without any action or motion of its own, knew by nature, immovably and substantially, all things that it can understand, and as a creature became in an instant full and perfect with the knowledge of all things. But since the human intellect was created in ignorance and privation of all things, and was temporally destined for a body for its own exercise, it must by continual action, motion, and art come to knowledge of God and of all things. The end will at last make it equal to the angelic intellect, changing its potency into act and bringing it from the merely potential and possible into essence; from empty it will make it full, from imperfect perfect, from deprived possessing, from dark luminous, from nocturnal diurnal, from lunar solar, from earthly heavenly. This cannot happen while the mind is bound in the body, as the holy Christ-loving Paul says: As long as we are in the flesh, we are pilgrims away from the Lord.

To know God belongs to a pure, simple, and perfect intellect. But the human intellect, as long as it dwells in the body, is impure, mixed, unstable, and imperfect; for this reason it is ignorant of the knowledge of God, namely of that highest thing among things. But the object of each intellect, namely both the human and the angelic, is the same: God, the supreme and single good of all things, toward which [unclear]; God, the single principle of things, toward which [unclear]. with a natural inclination toward cognition. But if the angelic intellect is compared with the human, it is as nature is to art, and as intellect simply speaking is to reason, which is closely joined to the principles of the disciplines, while reason proceeds discursively from principles to conclusions. Hence it is clear that the angelic intellect apprehends its proper object immovably; toward that object the human intellect, through the angelic medium, after many exercises of itself, as has been said, at last prepares an ascent for itself by reasoning. But the human intellect is separated, by the medium of angelic cognition, from the perfection of its natural object, and therefore is necessarily mobile, returning through that medium to its own principle. For every motion is made from one extreme through a middle to an extreme; but where there is no middle, the extremes are already immediate and proximate, and for this reason immobile. But the human intellect, placed as it were in a dark prison so long as it is held in the body, is moved by sense and reason toward understanding, although very confusedly and imperfectly; and for that reason it admits between itself and God the medium that we have called angelic, while it bears the body as the very great impediment to its destined perfection. As a certain lover of wisdom said: The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation depresses the sense that thinks many things. Therefore it was altogether necessary for us to believe in God rather than to know or understand him, because it is utterly impossible for that super-divine and uncircumscribable majesty to be comprehended by us, who understand nothing without the service of the senses and the discourse of reason. But God, existing far above every position, remains subject neither to the senses of mortals nor to reason, as he is read to have said to Moses: No man shall see me and live. Hence also the divine evangelist John says: No one has ever seen God. Nor is this any wonder. For since God is the first and everlasting intellect, most pure, most simple, most perfect, immobile, the creator, incomprehensible, highest, and far above every position, immeasurable and uncircumscribable, he could not be comprehended by the human intellect, which is impure, subject to composition, imperfect, mobile, created, comprehensible, lowest, and established under the measure of position.

¶ But concerning that question which seemed to arise from the first, whether God, since he is omnipotent, could have made himself knowable to the human intellect just as to the angelic, I say that no one of sound mind has ever denied that God can do all things. But those things that imply contradiction we say God cannot do, because they are contrary to the order of wisdom that immutably disposes all things, just as they are not doubted to be contrary to the destruction of the whole, and, if I may say so, utterly opposed to it. For it neither was fitting, nor could in any way have happened, that God should be comprehended by the human intellect; since if mortal man, by the dictate of nature, comprehended immortal God, certainly he would no longer seem to have to be called man or mortal, but an angel, and either man would become comparable to God or God to man. For as long as the angelic intellect stands between, the human cannot understand God. And it stands between until the death of the flesh, when the mind, having obtained its natural liberty, escapes wholly equal to the angel. You see now, I believe, emperor, that it is clear that it neither was fitting nor was possible that the human intellect should comprehend the divine: the created comprehend the creator, the temporal the eternal, the mutable the immutable, the weak the omnipotent, since, as a certain philosopher says, there is no proportion of the finite to the infinite. Therefore it is necessary for mortals to believe in immortal God, whom we can comprehend by no manifest reasoning. Although the order of the whole universe declares an author who provides for all things, and although we understand nothing besides him to have been brought forth into being without a beginning, nevertheless what God is and in what manner he is, the human mind cannot grasp:

Since he is far above all things that we, or any mortal, can understand concerning him, he is far beyond, outside, and above every affirmation, as holy Dionysius says. For he is neither soul nor sense; nor does he have imagination or opinion, or reason or understanding; nor is he reason or understanding; nor is he spoken of or understood. Nor is he number, multitude, order, magnitude, smallness, equality, likeness, or unlikeness; nor does he stand or move; nor does he bring about rest or have power; nor is he power or light; nor does he live, nor is he life, substance, age, or time. There is no spiritual contact with him; he is not form, truth, kingdom, wisdom, one, unity, deity, authority, or spirit, so far as we can know him. Nor is there a designation of Son or Father; nor is he anything else among those things known to us or to anyone else in the world. Nor is he anything of the things that are not, nor of the things that are; nor do the things that are know him as he himself is. Nor is there speech, name, or knowledge of him; nor is he darkness or light, error or truth; nor is there any affirmation or negation of him at all. For he, the perfect and singular cause of all things, is above every affirmation; and his excellence is above every negation, namely the excellence of him who is simply free from all things and above all things.

Therefore, Dionysius says, we say that since he is the cause of all things above all things, he is neither without substance nor without life; nor does he lack reason or mind; nor is he body, figure, or species; nor does he have quality, quantity, or mass. Nor is he in a place, nor is he seen; nor does he have sensible touch; nor does he sense, nor is he sensible; nor is he subject to rashness or disturbance, agitated by fleshly passions. Nor is he weak, subject to sensible accidents; nor is he in need of light; nor does he admit change, corruption, division, or flux; nor is he, or does he have, any other thing belonging to sensible things.

Hence, since he is far above every affirmation, excelling what is posited, he could not be comprehended by a creature that necessarily uses the senses for understanding, as the true Peripatetic said: nothing is in our intellect unless it has first been in the sense. Therefore God, who is not subject to the senses of mortals, far exceeds human understanding. According to affirmative positing he is truly altogether in all things; and according to negative removal, the nearer one approaches, he is none of all the things that are subject to mortal knowledge. Indeed, since he is above all things, he can be none of those things that are subject to him. Therefore Empedocles beautifully gave a likeness, saying: God is a sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. Let human understanding now lift itself as far as it can; and let whoever strives to comprehend God rightly understand and comprehend the center of this imagined sphere, together with its circumference ending nowhere. But if he is not able to understand this proposition of the likeness properly, why does he strive to investigate the essence of God, which exists above every affirmation?

Most unconquered Caesar, may it not weary you to hear another likeness concerning God from Cusanus, formerly cardinal priest of the Roman Church, my fellow Mosellan, a man most learned in those times, who says: God is a straight line of infinite length, which makes a circle. Now then let us see: if it is a straight line, how does it make a circle? But if it makes a circle, how is it straight? For a circle and a straight line are naturally opposed. Nevertheless, a line of infinite length, since it has neither beginning nor end, necessarily makes a circle, although it is proposed to be imagined not as curved but as straight. Since therefore God is infinite, greatest without quantity, best without quality, all things in all things without circumscription, above all things without an excluding position: It was not possible, therefore, that he should be comprehended by the circumscribed human intellect, which uses the service of the senses for understanding, or that what is promised to it when at last purified in the fatherland should be granted to it, confused and impure, on the way. But after our mind, at last released from the flesh, has escaped to its own center, which is God, clean, simple, pure, perfect, and consummated, and we have been made equal to the angels, we shall know God perfectly, and all things, just as the holy Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma; but then face to face.” Therefore we said that the angelic intellect, by the guidance of nature, adheres immovably to its own principle, because it is pure act and habit; and since it is naturally simple in condition, it can be hindered by no commerce of composition. But the human intellect, as it is now sufficiently clear has been explained, since it is potentiality and privation, is impure because of its commerce with its body; indeed it is held back from perfect act until at last, released from the flesh, it has passed into the fellowship of likeness with the angels, then for the first time to be admitted to the true knowledge of God. But if meanwhile the affection of love, necessary for salvation, is joined to present Christian faith and future divine knowledge, the same eternal blessedness prepared for the worshippers of God will be granted together with the holy angels. But if a depraved mind, through too much commerce with its flesh, has scorned the love of God, then indeed the intellect, released from its prison-house, will escape to the sublime knowledge belonging to it by nature according to its measure; but it will be the more wretched, the more by evil will it is found to be like the demons. Therefore, to conclude as best I may the solution of the question proposed, I say that it is not possible for almighty God to be perfectly understood by us so long as, mortal, we dwell in the flesh.

ON FAITH NECESSARY FOR SALVATION: The Second Question.

Question Second

The second question of your unconquered majesty was this: Since today only a small part of the world is subject to the laws of the Christian faith, whether that opinion of very many people seems admissible without injury to the truth, namely, of those who think that each person, in his own religion which he believes to be true and saving, as a worshipper of one God, can be saved outside the Christian faith without baptism, provided that he knows nothing of the religion of Christ.

To answer this question simply, according to the common understanding, I judged superfluous, since I know that today many among Christians, through a sort of impious piety for the salvation of lost men, make themselves cruel toward God. But because the cause of just consideration moved your most serene highness to ask these things, not because you do not know what must be held as Catholic in this position, but so that you might have something true to set against those who attack it, I shall answer the questions as briefly as I can. If anyone could be saved outside the Christian faith, Christ, the Son of almighty God, would seem to have been made man superfluously and without cause. For if there is salvation outside Christ, Christ is not the savior of all. But because it was necessary, according to the Scriptures, that the only-begotten Son of God, for the salvation of the human race, be born as a man in the world, suffer, die, and rise again on the third day, he did not come into this world in vain, nor superfluously, nor without cause. Since this is so, whoever asserts that anyone can be saved outside the faith of Christ shows himself not a Christian, but an adversary of the faith and a deserter of Christ. For whoever does not believe in Christ the Son of God promises himself eternal salvation in vain. For he himself, Jesus Christ, who is the truth, says in the holy Gospel: “He who does not believe is already judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. And again, a little later, he adds, saying: “He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.” Saint Christophylus also says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God.”

The solution to the proposed question is now clear to all who truly believe in Christ: salvation is through him, the Savior of the world, and whoever does not believe in him cannot be saved. Nor is it permitted for a Christian in any way to go beyond the limits of his religion, so as to presume to explain this question otherwise than Christ taught. But whoever departs from this rule of faith by asserting the contrary plainly shows that he does not think rightly concerning Christ, the Savior of the faithful. For whoever promises salvation to anyone outside Christ wishes to declare Christ a liar.

But we, confirmed by the most sacred ordinances of the Gospel, firmly believe and declare without doubt that no one outside the faith of Christ can be saved, however much he worships one God, however holy or justly he lives, however much he trusts in his paternal religion or another. Christ is salvation, and outside the Christian faith no one will be saved. For why did Christ, the Son of God, wish to die for the sins of the world, if each person could have been saved outside faith in him, in his own paternal tradition? From the beginning of the world, after the fall of the human race, it was impossible for anyone to be saved to eternal life otherwise than in the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, he says.

For what of the fact that the greater part of mankind remains outside the faith of Jesus today? Did not the Savior of the world himself long ago foretell in the holy Gospel that many are called, but few are chosen? And again he says: “Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and spacious is the way that leads to perdition, and many are those who enter through it.” What, we ask, can our salvation contribute to God, who has no need of our goods? For whether many are saved or damned, God himself is the immutable Lord of all; nothing is added to him if all are saved; nothing is lacking if the whole world perishes.

The order of divine providence and majesty is infallible; it embraces those who are to be damned no less than those who are to be saved, each and all. Certainly no one among the damned suffers injury, since, just as in the first man we all fell, so no one is saved except in the blood of Jesus Christ through mercy, and no one is damned except in his own unbelief and by desert through justice.

From what has been set forth, another question of no small difficulty arises, which human curiosity is accustomed to raise against those who think rightly concerning the faith of Christ: Why does almighty God, since he is just and merciful, not cease to create so many thousands of men whom he most certainly foreknew were to be damned? Why does he not spare the wretched, and not bring forth into destruction in so great a multitude those whom he foreknew would turn aside to evil? For it would seem better not to be than to be evilly.

To this question let him answer who thinks himself God’s counselor. Who am I, that I should explain the cause of the divine will? For all things whatsoever the Lord willed, he made in heaven and on earth; there is no one who can resist his will. Hence a certain wise man says to God: “Who will charge it to you if the nations that you made perish?” The almighty has established an order of alternation for things, which he will never revoke by any fullness of change. For just as he permits his sun to rise upon the good and the evil, so until the end of the age he allows men to be conceived, born, and grow, the pious and the impious. The thoughts of men are not in God, nor does he change his counsel according to time; but since he is immutable and eternal, willing all things together and at once and always, he has from eternity unchangeably preordained them. God speaks once, as Scripture bears witness, and does not add; since whatever he wills, he wills immovably and admits no change. Therefore, that men should be born good and evil, pious and impious, faithful and faithless, sinners and saints, those to be saved and those to be damned, occurs by a most just reason God permits this, who assigned this order to all things. Nothing is lost to God, who is Lord of all, and who holds his dominion everywhere, confirmed no less over evil men and spirits than over good ones. Christ Jesus, God from God the Father outside time, and man from the Virgin in time, appointed mediator between God and human beings, is himself the one through whom we have access to God. He is the Savior of all the faithful; and anyone thinks wrongly of him who rashly grants that anyone at all can be saved without the Christian faith. The omnipotence of God respects the order of things which he established; according to its inviolable sequence of rectitude, no one will be saved without faith in Christ; no one who does not believe in the Son of God is justified. Therefore those are moved by vain and utterly foolish piety who think that anyone outside the faith of Christ, in the whole world and in any sect whatever, is to be saved, since this is plainly contrary to his sentence.

Let them hear the Savior himself again saying in the Gospel: No one comes to the Father except through me. For I am the way, the truth, and the life. If no one comes to the Father except through the Son, certainly no one will be saved except through him. Who will save the Jew and the pagan, since no one can be saved except through Christ? But Christ will undoubtedly save only those who believe in him with heart, speech, and deed. He will not save the Jew, not the Saracen, not the pagan, not any other unbeliever, because he does not believe in him; rather, they despise his doctrine, contemn the faith, and, blaspheming his holy name, vilify it all day long. For he himself said in the Gospel: Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, I also shall be ashamed of him before my Father and his holy angels.

Tell me now, you who worship Christ and contend that someone can be saved outside the Christian faith in his own sect, which he thinks true: do you believe the Gospel of Christ to be true or false? If true, why do you think contrary to it? For Christ says: Whoever has not believed in the Son of God, the wrath of God remains upon him; and he has already been judged and will be condemned; and that no one comes to the Father except through me. But you, seduced by I know not what rashness, thrust in the contrary, saying that a man outside the faith of Christ, trusting in his ancestral religion, which he believes to be true and pleasing to God, or living innocently according to the law of nature, especially since perhaps he has never heard anything about the faith of Christ, is to be saved in that confidence. Christ did not say this, but: Whoever believes in the only-begotten Son of God will be saved; but whoever does not believe has already been judged. He excepted no one; he admitted no condition, since he who had come to suffer for all had provided for the salvation of all through faith alone. If faith in the Savior is lacking, then no confidence will save the unbeliever.

For the holy bishop Augustine said in On Faith to Peter: Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in any way, that not only all pagans, but also all Jews, heretics, and schismatics who end this present life outside the catholic Church will go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels. You see now where foolish compassion draws you: you who measure God by human laws, so that you may make him merciful in all things, do not fear to judge his only-begotten Son, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, a liar. But Christ is truthful, who says that those who do not believe in him are to be damned; you, however, are rash and liars, because you trust that someone can be saved outside his faith. Whoever truly believes in Christ does not permit anyone at all outside the unity of the catholic Church of Christians to be said to be saved. Who says the contrary? For this is the inviolable sentence of catholic tradition, which the Lord Jesus himself, the Son of God, defined in the holy Gospel: namely, that no one is to be saved outside his faith, which he himself instituted, taught, and confirmed by his own blood. Therefore whoever says that a man is to be saved in any sect whatever outside the faith of Jesus Therefore, whoever has affirmed, or has believed in his heart, that a person is to be saved in any sect outside the faith of Jesus Christ, is not a good Christian, but rather an apostate and a disciple of Antichrist; unless he comes to his senses, let him know that he is to be tormented forever in hell with him. For he is an Antichrist, not a Christian, who says that one who does not believe in the Lord Jesus is to be saved without the Savior. Therefore, most wise Caesar, let no one appear in the sight of your majesty, and let no one sense that you adhere to him, who thinks that people are to be saved outside the faith of Jesus Christ. For everyone who has believed that anyone is to be saved outside the faith of Christ has denied both Christ and his Gospel.

But when we say that all who are not Christians are to be damned, this is a sign not of cruelty but of true piety. For it is better to believe firmly in the truth than to assent falsely to a human being. That all Jews, pagans, gentiles, Saracens, schismatics, heretics, and unbelievers are without doubt to be damned eternally with the demons is attested by the holy Church, which took and confirmed this judgment from no other source than from the words of Christ. For thus he said: “He who believes in the Son has eternal life,” by which the faith and work of a good Christian are signified. “But he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.” Here all Jews, pagans, Saracens, gentiles, and all who do not believe in our Lord Jesus Christ are designated. Concerning schismatics and heretics, however, Christ’s judgment is manifest in the Gospel, where he says: “If he refuses to hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican.” Heathens are gentiles; publicans are manifest and public sinners, of whose utterly certain damnation the holy Church does not doubt. For who among Christians would doubt that gentiles and monstrous and manifest sinners are to be damned? Since, therefore, all schismatics and heretics despise the Church of the saints, they are most rightly said to be like the gentiles and publicans who are to be damned for their crimes and deserts, and they will justly undergo with them equal punishments of everlasting damnation.

Behold those whom the just sentence of Christ the Savior has damned: does the foolish compassion of men, not to say impious cruelty, presume that they are to be saved? They desire to be merciful toward lost men, and do not fear to show themselves cruel toward God. Those whom he, by justice, has assigned to death, they assert, by the worst presumption, are to be recalled to life. It is neither good nor useful for a Christian, whether in earnest or in jest, to contradict Christ. He is impious, not a Christian, whoever says that unbelievers are to be saved.

When Adam, the first man, perished, we all sinned, and the wrath of God remained upon the whole human race from the beginning of the world until Christ. Christ came, born of a virgin; being God and man, innocent of sin, he voluntarily underwent the death of the cross, and, having become mediator between God and man, removed the wrath of original guilt from those who believe in him. For thus he says: “He who believes in the only-begotten Son of God has eternal life. But he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life; rather, the wrath of God remains upon him.” Indeed, without faith in Jesus Christ no one will be saved, however justly and holily he may seem to live in his own religion. For almighty God can save a believer without material baptism, but he cannot save one who denies without faith. No one is saved unwillingly, because no one believes unless willingly. For the Lord knows who are his, since he saves those who believe in the Son through repentance, but condemns unbelievers by the equity of justice.

Hence, while these matters were closed off, a new question struck the mind. What is to be thought about the infants and fools of unbelieving pagans and Jews? To this one must answer briefly. Just as the infants of Christians, baptized in the faith of their parents, are saved, so the unbaptized children of all unbelievers will be damned in the perfidy of their parents. The judgment concerning fools of either religion is similar: just as we believe without doubt that baptized fools of Christians are to be saved, so we should say without doubt that those of unbelievers are to be damned.

B iij Again here he asks what, according to Catholic teaching, is to be thought about those people who inhabit the newly discovered islands in the great sea, of which no mention is made among the old cosmographers, and who, as we have been informed, have never heard anything at all of the Christian religion. A brief answer is given, conforming in all respects to what has been written before: Truth has utterly excepted from damnation no one who does not believe: not an islander, not one contiguous with our world, not anyone else, whether dwelling near or far away; but without distinction and without limitation of persons he concluded, saying, “He who believes and has been baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned,” and the wrath of God remains upon him.

Who removes the wrath of God from man, except our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the mediator between God and men? By what means, except through faith formed in him who, though innocent, tasted death? Since, therefore, no one is saved without faith, we cannot promise salvation to those ignorant of Christ, since it is clear that they do not have the piety of faith in him. Necessarily, then, we shall say that all who do not believe in the Son of God are damned, whether they have heard of him or are wholly ignorant of him.

Yet we grant one thing: if any among those who are ignorant of Christ lived well according to the law of nature, invoking one God, even if they sometimes sinned, provided they had done penance before death, they have been or are to be less gravely damned than those who either hear of Christ and despise him, or who among either group lived wickedly and foully. For God is just; he does wrong to no one, but renders to each according to his works. But the wrath of God remains upon everyone who does not believe in his only-begotten Son, because of the original sin of the first man, from which no one is justified except through faith and the baptism of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. But if original sin alone is present in a person, as in little children, unless it is removed through Christ it condemns the one who has it to the penalty of loss only, by which, namely, he is barred from the vision of God and from the enjoyment of the happiness of the saints forever. But an adult who sins mortally will be punished after death with a double penalty, namely of loss and of sense, so that he both does not see God and, feeling the pains of the fire of Gehenna without end, never escapes them.

Jews, however, and Saracens, and all the rest who hear the faith of Christ and despise it are without doubt damned to both penalties, of loss and of sense, whether otherwise they live innocently according to the law of nature or the contrary. But among those who have never had any hearing of Christ, if any should live innocently according to the law of nature until death, I do not think they have furnished cause for it to be said or believed that they are to be damned to the penalty, although they are deprived forever of the vision of God, which theologians have called the penalty of the damned. For no one will behold the face of God the Father almighty unless he has been reborn through faith in Christ.

¶ Now let us pronounce judgment against those who, when we assert these things in Catholic fashion according to Christ’s doctrine, object with foolish reflection: Why did God, since he is supremely good, wish to create so many thousands of human beings whom he foreknew from eternity would be damned? For if Christians are compared with unbelievers, scarcely a twentieth part of the people of the whole world today believes in our Lord Jesus Christ. The boundless curiosity of this question has often struck many; if their faith in Christ were firm and their devotion fervent in love for him, they would not ask things so unusual and difficult. For who is found among mortals of such honor in learning or holiness that, apart from God himself, he might disclose to us the cause of the divine will? The will of God is incomprehensible, because he himself is the cause of his most righteous will. The everlasting order is inviolable; and, as I said above, God does wrong to no one.

When God judged that a universal flood should come upon the earth, were not only eight people saved in the ark, while all the rest perished by the inundation of the waters? The cause of their being struck down was sin. That they were created had no other cause than the uncircumscribable goodness of God. That few are saved while many perish, a figure preceded the mystery; and Noah’s ark [was a figure] of the Christian faith sacrament. For indeed, just as all perished in the flood outside Noah’s ark, so now all who are outside the unity of the catholic Church of Christians will without doubt perish eternally in their sins: Jews as well as pagans, heretics likewise and schismatics. The justice of God condemns those whom his goodness created. But mercy saves those whom grace has confirmed, because, as the holy Apostle says, it is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy; for he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. If we rightly weigh the freedom of human choice, we shall also know the just will of God.

ON THE MIRACLES

Of Unbelievers. Third Question.

Question Third

The third question of your most serene majesty was: If no one is saved outside the faith, whence come miracles among unbelievers, since we know from the report of many that astonishing things occur even among unbelievers?

The solution of this question, as it seems to me, will not be difficult if we give credence both to the Scriptures and apply the necessary consideration to the natural powers of the soul. A miracle is a new and unusual event, which occurs beyond ordinary custom and draws human beings into wonder. Hence good Christians perform miracles in one way, bad Christians in another, and unbelievers in yet another. Good Christians perform miracles through public righteousness; bad Christians, however, through signs of public righteousness; but unbelievers through private contracts with demons, that is, implicit or explicit ones. Concerning the good, indeed, the Lord said in the holy Gospel: These signs shall follow those who have believed. In my name they shall cast out demons; they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it shall not harm them. They shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall be well.

Concerning bad Christians, however, who perform miracles in the name of Jesus Christ, we read thus written in the Gospel: Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name done many mighty works? And then I shall declare to them: I never knew you; depart from me, all you who work iniquity. But outside the Church of God, where the name of our Lord Jesus Christ is not invoked, if any marvels are done beyond the custom of nature or human art, no good Christian doubts that they are done by the cooperation of demons. And works of this sort your Caesarean Serenity, by discernment of power, judges should rather be called marvels than miracles. Nor does this judgment depart from the reason of truth, insofar as there should be a necessary distinction between the prodigies of light and of darkness.

I find four agents of wondrous things, but I recognize one alone, God, who truly works miracles, chiefly as the cause of all good things. Therefore the first and greatest agent of all marvels is God, who has illuminated the whole world by filling it with signs, miracles, and mighty works; none of the rest is to be compared with him. He created heaven and earth, the sea and all things that are in them; he alone is omnipotent, just, holy, and upright; good, incomprehensible, greatest, glorious, immeasurable, and everlasting. Let all other things be beneath him, for whatever can happen wondrously in this world is certainly less than the whole world itself, which he was able to create from nothing. Every miracle, too, that can be done through a human being is less than the human being himself, whom God, the creator of all things, formed from the beginning in his own image and likeness. And although the visible miracles of God among mortals, through the constant habit of seeing natural things, have now almost become commonplace, nevertheless, if we behold them wisely, they will appear greater and rarer than all unusual things. But the manner in which God performs miracles is the unchangeable will of God, which, since it is omnipotent, does all things whatsoever it has willed in heaven and on earth. For he himself spoke, and they were made. Cj They were made; he himself commanded, and they were created. The will of God is ordered and everlasting; therefore his miracles are incomparably greater than all others. For greater than all the miracles of this world is what we behold: the whole universe, and whatever is contained in it, created by the will of God. The unchangeable divine will works all things, enduring, because it lacks both beginning and end. But whatever God wills, he always wills; since in him to will and to be able are the same, labor does not belong to the unchangeable one. Thus all the universal miracles that the Creator of all things performs he has presented for good and evil alike to behold; and after the general miracles, which have now grown cheap among mortals through familiarity, he has also shown, in almost every single creature, countless things especially worthy of wonder.

The second performer of miracles is the good angel, who very often works wonders for mortals both by natural virtue and by divine power. For those most blessed spirits are sent by divine ordinance in ministry to the faithful; they furnish to both good and evil the things that are benefits of nature, but only to those who believe in God and our Lord Jesus Christ do they administer the gifts of saving grace. Hence there is no doubt that those miracles which are done in the Church of the saints by invocation of the divine name are displayed by their ministry and cooperation. But the wonders of unbelievers, if any are done today or are read to have been done formerly, are either fabricated or falsely reported, or are accomplished by the mockery of demons. For it cannot happen that unbelievers perform any miracles by the ministry of good angels, since where Christ Jesus, the Son of God, is not believed, no signs of grace are displayed by good spirits to impious and reprobate men. Indeed, since they are obstinate in the error of a false religion, if in their own estimation they have obtained any miracle, there is no reason whatever to doubt that it is done through the ministry of demons. For since they are wholly unlike the good angels, they attain no familiarity with them. No despiser of the Christian faith can please God; but whoever is shown to displease almighty God is without doubt deprived of the familiarity of the holy angels. Yet by this I do not take back the claim that every human being has been entrusted to some good spirit, by whose ministry, even if he is unbelieving toward the Son of God, he may receive the benefits of nature, though he may not attain the gifts of grace. But to those who believe in our Lord Jesus Christ they confer not only the benefits of nature, but also administer the gifts of grace. It is therefore manifest that, if any miracles are done among unbelievers, they cannot be done by the gift of God or by the ministry of the holy angels, since all are placed outside the unity of the Church, and signs cannot be worked by the impious through public righteousness. For God, as has been said, does not remove his original wrath from man except through faith in Jesus Christ; but everyone who is unbelieving toward the Son of God will not see eternal life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. Therefore everyone upon whom the wrath of God remains will not be able to please him; and so, if any wondrous things are done at his prayers, they should be believed to have been performed not by the power of God nor by the ministry of angels, but rather by the intervention of demons.

The third performer of wonders is the devil, who, like an ape, is eager to imitate whatever he has seen, and deceives the minds of men, especially unbelievers, with various illusions; and he believes that, by a certain likeness of miracles, he can seduce those who believe in him, for it is agreed that they were created by nature subtler than all mortals. They cannot know the thoughts of mortals except by a kind of conjecture, when, that is, our inward things are made manifest by certain signs. Demons foretell future things, and sometimes they speak truly; sometimes, making conjectures, they are deceived and deceive. From the beginning of the world they have known certain signs that precede events; by experience and use of these signs they sometimes foretell as true what is going to happen, because when they have seen signs known to themselves preceding a matter, they immediately conjecture what is in a person's thought. Yet more often they deceive, because they themselves are also deceived. For when concerning some when they are asked about a matter which they do not know: for example, whether a messenger sent far away will return soon, or on what day. Immediately, in the blink of an eye, they arrive at the place where they know him to be; and when they have seen that he has already begun the journey of return, they carefully count the stages, and, suddenly returning to the questioner, affirm that the absent man will come on a definite day. But if he has either delayed on the road or turned aside elsewhere, then certainly the demons, now deceived in their own judgment, must be mistaken.

They gladly involve themselves in prophecies, and are quite ready to foretell future things to human beings for the sake of honor and esteem, since they very much desire to be regarded as worthy of admiration. They seek divine honors, and greatly desire to be feared by mortals. Just as boys, hiding in secret or running about masked, suddenly burst out from their hiding places and shake with unexpected terror their companions, who suspect no such thing, and then hide themselves again lest they be recognized; when they see the unsuspecting ones terrified, they boast as if they had obtained some great honor from this. After the example of these, certain demons, more bound to the earth and very restless, who move about among human beings, whom the ancients called Bacucei, terrify people at night; and they seek nothing more from mortals than the reputation of divinity. Hence also, before those with whom they are permitted to be by reason of likeness, they sometimes perform various tricks, and present themselves as terrifying in people’s minds as occasion permits. Whenever they can, they gladly clothe themselves in the likeness of a human body; but they do not always find suitable material of air with which to be clothed. For this reason they often appear monstrous and horrible, because they have not had suitable humors or vapors for perfecting the appearance they desired. But the more they are bound to earthly dwellings, the more, by that circumstance, they have been made dull with respect to matter. Hence, because of the ignorance which they contracted through disobedience, the predictions of demons are frequently false, although by divine permission they are sometimes even verified.

For, as that most holy John Chrysostom says, it is sometimes granted to the devil to speak the truth, so that he may commend his lie by rare truth; because if he never spoke the truth, he could deceive no one, and his seduction would by no means suffice for tempting. It is therefore not astonishing if demons sometimes seem to foretell true things to unbelieving human beings, since they once could offer prophecies to the gentiles in idols. Nor is it astonishing if they sometimes provide care for the sick, since they know the natures of all herbs and can very easily apply themselves to the ill, and either remove diseases which they had previously inflicted, or for a time withdraw from the senses those which chance has inflicted. For almighty God, by the right of imperial majesty over all things, uses even the ministry of demons both for the testing of the faithful and for the punishment of the impious. Since they are perverse in affection, obstinate in their rebellion, and proud, they greatly desire divine esteem and honors; and therefore they gladly answer the invocations of unbelievers which they are accustomed to pour out to the gods, as if they themselves were gods.

Among unbelievers they sometimes seem to raise the dead to life, and they show marvelous things to curious people, so that they may render them altogether obstinate in their former error, as if confirmed by miracles. Yet they do not truly raise the dead, but deceive the senses of human beings in various ways: for either they themselves enter the corpses of the dead and carry them about for a time as if alive, or, after those bodies have been taken away to a more remote place, they display to the spectators some image in the appearance of the person who has departed life, as the experience of certain people has informed us. We believe it manifest that demons can show, in a certain false likeness, all the things whatsoever that the saints do as miracles in truth. All the miracles of demons are either phantasms, or things done by a certain natural skill. For if human beings in the more hidden matters of nain the mysteries of nature, by a certain application of matter to form that is hidden from others, produce unusual and wondrous effects, such as forming natural eels from the dew of heaven, bees from calves’ flesh, serpents from certain roots of herbs, and many things similar to these, not to mention greater things, as experiment has made us experienced in very many cases, who would deny that demons, subtler in nature and of greater experience, can naturally accomplish more wondrous things that are manifest to no human beings?

The fourth worker of miracles, however, is man, who works wonders in four ways, which to those who know neither the cause nor the manner do not seem human. First, indeed, by invocation of the divine name, when in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ there concurs the merit of accepted holiness. In this way the holy apostles and their imitators, by the power of God and likewise by the merit of holiness, wrought miracles in the unity of faith. But in this way unbelievers cannot work miracles, for they do not walk the necessary path of faith unto salvation. For even if many of them believe in one God, nevertheless, because they refuse to believe in the mediator between God and men, they have gone very far away from the mercy of God.

But, as the holy Gospel promises, all things are possible for those who believe in God and our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, for those who also adorn right faith with holy works. For indeed, just as without faith it is impossible to please God, so also faith without works is dead. For almighty God would grant us all the things that we ask in the faith of Christ, if we did all things according to the faith that we owe. Believe firmly and act faithfully, and you will always obtain all things.

Second, a man works miracles by likeness to angelic purity. For the purer our mind becomes through love, confirmed in the faith of Jesus Christ, so much the more, made like to the holy angels, does it attain greater familiarity with them. Whoever, however, has attained complete familiarity with the holy angels, when he wishes, by God’s bounty, he will shine forth in miracles.

For the holy angels reveal to pure men, and to those fervent in the love of God, secrets hidden from others, and by command of the Creator they make many things manifest to them. For the Lord is near to those who call upon him in truth. The Lord will do the will of those who fear him; and he will hear their prayers and save them. For whoever through grace is one with Christ is refreshed by the frequent visitation of angels; and, as often as necessity requires it, he is made illustrious by signs and powers through their ministry.

Hence it is that those also who are weighed down by various illnesses betake themselves to the intercessions of the saints; and, calling to mind the promises of the Lord, they obtain by another’s merits what they cannot obtain by their own. Their holy devotion in the faith of Christ receives salvation from the Lord; for, aided by the purity of its own conscience and supported by the merit of another’s holiness, it rises, not rashly, into sure hope.

Miracles, however, occur in the Church of God by divine power with a threefold regard or means. For sometimes almighty God works a miracle by the ministry of angels, solely by the merits of the worker himself, as Saint Martin healed a blind man and a lame man against their will. Sometimes miracles occur by the merit of the sufferer alone, as we read that many were cured through bad Christians whom the sick believed to be very good in the faith. Third, that healings of this kind occur by the merits of both is to be held, since Christ says to a certain person in the holy Gospel: If you can believe, all things are possible to the believer. For faith is always required for a miracle, so that our Lord Jesus Christ, coming into his own country, wondered that he could not do any mighty work there because of their unbelief. But none of these things is done among unbelievers, where neither holiness in the worker nor orthodox faith in the sufferer is found.

Third, therefore, a man works miracles through the intervening cooperation of diabolical depravity; and this can happen in three ways, namely by manifest involvement and supposition in the invocation of demons, Through manifest invocation necromancers and the little women whom we commonly call witches perform wondrous things, having been corrupted by likeness of will and passed into the fellowship of demons. For just as in the Church of God the sacraments are signs of the invisible grace of the Holy Spirit, so in the school of demons certain characters and modes of invocation are marks of a pact between a human being and an evil spirit. Hence, when witches display the signs of demons, the invoked evil spirits have commonly been glad to come to them and to exhibit both dreadful works of witchcraft and certain wondrous things.

But witches and necromancers produce wondrous effects by the invocation of demons in different ways. Witches subject themselves to demons by a certain kind of profession; by their ministry they trouble the air, raise storms, ravage crops, and make human beings and beasts ill. They carry on foul commerce of the filthiest pleasure with demons, and by pernicious charms call back from the lower world into sight whomever they wish. The deeds of these women should not be called miracles, but rather acts of witchcraft, and deservedly punished with the severest penalty.

Necromancers, however, subject themselves to demons not by a manifest profession, but by an implicit condition, when they promise to compel them to appear visibly in a circle, not only by conjurations and the display of characters, but also by sacrifices, fumigations, and vows. Their crimes are without number, since it is clear that all, whether implicitly or explicitly, conspire into the fellowship of demons. Although not all necromancers are equal in either art or practice, yet all are united, to their own destruction, by a damnable curiosity, by which they desire, with the aid of demons, to attain what they cannot discover naturally. All their works and volumes are full of superstitions and impiety, and for that reason must be driven far from the borders of believers.

There is in the East a great multitude of enchanters and necromancers, who by their illusions miserably deceive the human race, and long ago turned almost all Asia Major and Asia Minor away from the faith of Christ. Illusions can be produced in three ways: by the ministry of demons, by the operation of nature, and by the deception of human art. No true Christian will doubt that the miracles of unbelievers are produced in one of these ways, once the determinate root of the agent has been established. Today, moreover, there are many among Christians devoted to the works of demons: enchanters, witches, and those reprobate concerning the faith, who deceive many by excessive curiosity and promise impossibilities by their arts.

Through the implication of demons, however, wondrous things are sometimes done: namely, whenever a person not sufficiently and rightly grounded in the faith works for or wishes something otherwise than befits a Christian, even if he believes there is no sin in it; and although it ought not to happen, nevertheless the devil, inserting himself, very often supplies the desired effect. Such is the practice which sufferers from spasms commonly use. On the holy day of Parasceve, during the office, they fashion a ring of any metal, which they thereafter always wear on the heart-finger. These things are utterly vain and have no root of truth at all. Yet I cannot deny that I have seen some people cured of spasm by this same vanity.

Likewise, I know that certain men have opened very strong locks with words and herbs; I do not think this was done either by the power of God or by the force of the things applied. I could introduce countless similar cases which I have seen and heard: what else are their manifest effects but certain miracles? Finally, there are some exceedingly curious people who, by stubbornly placing faith and confidence in characters, slips, rings, figures, necklaces, and unknown words, often obtain wondrous effects. We by no means doubt that the devil has supplied these, not by merit of holiness nor by mercy granted by God, but rather through faithless credulity. For demons, having the greatest envy of the human race, gladly come to vain practices in order to destroy the souls of mortals. in the operations of the impious. For what else are characters and interpretations of hidden names than certain foods and drinks for demons? Whoever puts faith in characters that promise marvelous effects has implicitly denied both the faith of Christ and the Church of the saints. Alas, how many Christians today, how many clerics, how many priests, to spare those of higher rank, use many and various superstitions in their daily actions; through these they follow compacts with demons bound up in them, to the insult of the Christian faith and to their own condemnation. And because these evils have now multiplied too greatly among Christians, the Almighty has withdrawn his hand and handed them over into the dominion of the faithless, so that they may feel as exactors of punishments those in imitation of whom they were stubbornly serving, not the living and true God, but empty superstitions.

But that marvelous things are done by the substitution of demons we plainly recognize, if we inquire more carefully into the truth. For Jews, Saracens, pagans, or gentiles, who do not believe in our God Jesus Christ, if they perform any miracles, are believed to do them not by the power of God, not by the ministry of angels, not by the merit of holiness, but by the substitution of demons. For as often as they invoke almighty God, in whose only-begotten Son they do not believe, for the mercy of some marvelous effect, the devil, knowing that there is no salvation for sinners, and that the Most High does not hear unbelieving sinners, secretly applies himself in place of the God invoked, in order to keep them obstinate in their errors; and, if he can, with the Lord permitting it, he grants to those praying what is requested. The devil uses this substitution all the more freely, the less he is hindered by the faith of Christ and the sacraments of the Church. For the wrath of God remains upon all unbelievers who do not believe in his only-begotten Son; and they are in the power of the devil, and therefore, when invoked, he enters in place of God. Hence, blinded in their errors, they invoke God, in whose Son they do not believe; and when he, holding them in wrath, scorns to hear them, the devil, a false worker of wonders, comes near. Therefore they believe the mockeries of the devil, they who disdain to believe the true miracles of God. From demons they receive false miracles suited to their errors, who by believing were unwilling to follow the truth, that is, Christ. For there are many among the unbelievers who, worshiping one God, the creator of all things, do not adore idols, and firmly believe that they will be saved in their own faith. But because they disdain to believe the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, the wrath of God remains upon them, and they vanish away in their foolishness. Thinking God to be near to them, though they do not believe rightly in him, they are subjected to demons; and, putting faith in their false miracles, they are confirmed in their errors by falsehood.

It may not be wearisome to have introduced a likeness of this matter, O Caesar. There was a certain swineherd who had enclosed in a stick a small sheet containing the name of the holy martyr Blaise; he put such faith in it that he believed every wolf would be prevented from approaching if the staff were fixed in the ground in the middle of the herd. This foolish confidence, at last strengthened by long experience, made the man go safely wherever he wished, leaving the pigs in the wood without danger, since no wolf now had any access to a pig. It happened that a certain man passed by, while the shepherd was absent, and, seeing a demon keeping guard over the herd, said to him: “What are you doing here, wretched one?” He replied: “I am guarding these pigs.” But he said: “Who entrusted the care of pigs to you?” “The foolish confidence of the shepherd. For he enclosed a certain small sheet in a stick, thinking it to be of great piety and virtue, so that by the merits of some Blaise wolves might be kept away from the pigs; he has sinned against his own law and follows our vanities. But because the one invoked does not appear, I, lest the man lose his confidence, guard his pigs for him; and I willingly substitute myself for Blaise. Thus ungrateful mortals harass us with vain conjurations, so that, unless we wish to lose all esteem and honor among them, we must, I confess, often come in answer to their foolish invocations.” By the likeness of this deed demons deceive unbelievers. and the miracles that they ask of God when praying they more often attain through the substitution of malignant spirits. For in matters that concern the worship or honor of God, demons gladly thrust themselves in; and those who cannot obtain open honors take great delight in hidden ones.

At the same time it must be noted that from the beginning of the world no religion or sect of chief eminence has ever lacked miracles, although they have not all been done from one principle. For whatever miracles have been done in the true religion have been done from no source other than God. The law of nature had its miracles; the written law had them; grace now has them as well. The almighty God who gave religion also himself performs miracles. But in false religions, where truth is not worshiped, if any miracles are done, it is not God but the devil who works them. For since God is truth, he did not establish false religions; and therefore he has never made falsehood illustrious by his miracles. Mahomet, who, full of an evil demon, established a false religion, adorned it with false miracles not from God but by the cooperation of demons. For the demon who gave the cause of the error could also, once the occasion had been taken, display a false miracle to those deceived. Hence, if miracles had been wholly lacking to Mahomet as he was persuading a rude people of a new religion, perhaps no one would have put faith in him. For he too showed certain wondrous things to the peoples, as much by subtlety of intellect as by the cooperation of the devil, so that he seemed to have confirmed a new doctrine also by new miracles. Miracles were not lacking even to the idolatrous pagans, if we do not deny credence to histories. But the Jews, before the incarnation of the Son of God, receiving his law through Moses, were often made illustrious by divine miracles. Yet after the Lord's resurrection, when the Mosaic law had been made void, those who do not believe in the only-begotten Son of God remain under the wrath of his indignation; and all miracles of truth have ceased among them. Hence, if they do any wondrous things today, they are works of demons and manifest signs of error. For demons, with the greatest zeal, keep watch so that those men whom they have once made to wander from the way of truth, which is Christ, they may, by a continuation of fraud until death, make stubborn in error. Indeed, when God for just reason withdraws his grace from unbelievers, their deceiver, a malignant and unknown spirit, approaches; and when he sees that salvation is far away, by false miracles he seduces the minds of the ignorant, as though the Lord were near. Therefore whatever miracles belong to unbelievers are works of demons; for just as there is no salvation for mortals outside the unity of the Christian faith, so without Christ the most holy power does not grant wonders. For now the demons, hiding in ambush, long since defeated and confounded by the trophy of Christ, fear to appear openly as they did before the Lord's incarnation; and therefore among unbelievers they falsely present themselves as good spirits.

There are also some who add a fourth mode to the aforesaid three, saying that the mind or spirit of man himself can naturally do wondrous things, provided it knows how to recall itself from every adventitious thing into itself, above sense, into unity. For those who assert such things promise to perform the wonders of nature, to predict future things, to disclose men's secrets, to remove diseases, and suddenly to change men's counsels. But that mode of miracles cannot be simply natural, certain, common, and infallible; for if it is true, which I have not experienced, some external power must necessarily intervene and partly take possession of the one thinking, whether a good angel or a malignant spirit. But if none of the external powers mixes itself in, the one prophesying must necessarily form the beginning of his speech either from conjectures or from bold presumption, and pronounce a judgment sometimes true, sometimes false. Indeed, as long as the spirit dwells in the body, it naturally understands nothing without the ministry of sense. Hence I would not wholly resist if they grant that our confused and rude intellect is aided by a like ministry. For we see this in those who very often, from a desire of inward love for Jesus, of the flesh while contemplating the mode, pass beyond it: lifted upward from the earth into the air. We think that they surpass bodily weight not merely by their own keenness of mind, but nevertheless by divine power.

Therefore the three principles of the opinion just mentioned, unknown to many, in my judgment are enough for a few: that the mind, placed in the body, by its own power works wondrous effects outside itself. For what? Let anyone ignorant of nature tell me whether bodily weight can be lightened by the operation of the mind. I speak of a thing I experienced, with two others bearing witness with me. When, as a youth, I was pursuing literary studies, four of us were sleeping one night in a single bed. One of the same age arose, and, asleep as he was accustomed to do in dreams, walked about the house with his eyes closed, the full moon shining within, almost as if he were awake. He climbed walls and outdid a squirrel in his agility. He also, while asleep, crossed over the bed a second and a third time; he trod on all of us with his feet, and we felt no greater weight than if some little thing had touched us. Wherever his sleeping body moved, suddenly all the fastenings of the doors opened of their own accord. He very swiftly passed through the higher parts of the house and clung to the roofs like a sparrow. I speak of things seen, not heard by vague report.

These seem to be functions of the soul, not of the body: the soul, by its natural power, so to speak, uses itself almost freely when, the senses of the flesh being bound, it wanders outside the dwelling place of the body. But since this matter is not in every respect suited to the question proposed, let us put off the treatment of the causes of these marvels to another time. For we do not believe that these things are wondrous to wise men, who have very well understood the power and nobility of the human mind, since, hindered only by the interposition of the body, in other respects it is judged equal to angels. Finally, let us pass over fascinations and their various modes and kinds, by which a very furious man works externally very wondrous effects. The imagination of one who trusts very strongly also has much power for producing wondrous effects, whether it is directed toward a true object or toward one imagined. Hence, since there are so many kinds and modes of working wonders, it is not surprising if Jews, Saracens, pagans, gentiles, and all the other unbelievers established outside the faith of Christ, who cannot perform miracles by public justice, carry out wonders either by the support of demons or by artful industry. Nor does it escape me that, by the same reasoning, the miracles of the saints are attacked by the impious, as if they were not done by the power of the Creator but rather by the involvement or substitution of the devil. Whoever truly believes that the Christian faith alone is true does not doubt that all the miracles of unbelievers have been performed by the cooperation of demons. But if anyone rashly and obstinately thinks the contrary, he shows himself to be an unbeliever, not a Christian.

ON SACRED SCRIPTURE

Sacred. Fourth Question.

Question Fourth

The fourth question of your most serene majesty was this: Why did almighty God not give sacred Scripture, containing the mysteries of our faith of both the New and the Old Testament, open, manifest, uniform in all things, plain, and sufficient for all things, but rather wrapped up and in many places full of enigmas? For many things necessary for the perfection of faith are not found sufficiently expressed in the divine Scriptures. To this most sacred question of your majesty, it seems that one must answer: Every Scripture divinely inspired is a perfect work of divinity, ordained before all time, written in time, in no other way than God willed, who inspired men that it should be written. But all the works of God are perfect; and therefore, since the Scripture about which we speak is the work of God, it is necessary to confess that it is perfect in all things. For the supreme judge, God, whose works are all perfect, willed it, and conferred upon his Scriptures the order that he willed; and without doubt he infused into those who received them the manner in which they should write.

For almighty God has conferred such authority and majesty upon Sacred Scripture that, in comparison with it, all the words of this world fail, since divine things cannot properly be comprehended by human speech. Divine Scripture, therefore, which on the surface of its words appears confused to the unlearned, seems manifest to those who know it; for unless it is read in that Spirit by which it is believed to have been infused into human beings, one by no means arrives at an understanding of it. The learned man who burns under the covering of the flesh and with vain desires reads it in one way; and the man of understanding, stripped of pleasures and truly inflamed by the love of God, reads it in another. Hence it is no wonder if men who savor carnal things do not understand the divine Scriptures, since, blinded by the pleasures of the flesh, they have never perceived the sweetness of the Spirit of God.

Just as, if you show to a boy learning the first elements of letters any written volume whose script is unlike that in his own little book, when he cannot read the writing he will at once cry out that the writing is bad and not rightly formed. In the same way, men who are wise only carnally approach the reading of the divine Scriptures; they do not grasp the things that belong to the divine Spirit, and, weighed down by vices and rashness, although they ought to have blamed their own ignorance and unworthiness, they censure as holy the Scriptures which they do not understand. For it is not permitted indiscriminately to all to interpret the divine Scriptures, lest the beast that touches the mountain be overwhelmed with stones.

Now there arise, in a disorderly order, many who have spent the whole span of their life on humane letters; and, having grown old, they interpret perversely the divine Scriptures which they never learned: they do not make them clear, but confuse them and discuss them according to their own sense. Hence all who do not understand the sacred Scriptures in that Spirit by which they were infused into those who wrote them have the veil of ignorance and rashness spread over their hearts, after the manner of the Jews; and from that source they often drink the poison of pernicious error, from which those who approach humbly in the Spirit of God have received the cup of salvation. For heavenly doctrine is not contained in the words of the Scriptures but in the meaning; not on the surface of utterances, but in the understanding; not in leaves adorned with ornament, but in the hidden place of mystical inspiration. Hence the divine pope Gregory says: Sacred Scripture far surpasses all the sciences of this world in its manner of speaking, because in one and the same discourse, while it narrates the text, it brings forth the mystery; and just as it refreshes the simple on the surface, so it exercises the wise in mystery. For it has openly that with which it may nourish little ones, and it keeps hidden that by which it may suspend the minds of the lofty in admiration of its sweetness, like a certain wondrous river in which both the simple little lamb may walk and the great elephant may swim. And Saint Augustine says on Genesis: Divine Scripture speaks in such a way that by its height it mocks the proud, by its depth it terrifies the attentive, by its power it feeds the great, and by its affability it nourishes the little.

For the authority of Sacred Scripture is greater than all the keenness of human talent. Therefore, in order that one may arrive at their true understanding, first of all the soul must be cleansed from every carnal affection; the help of divine goodness must be earnestly implored with humility, so that by his Spirit he may illuminate the understanding of the learner. For the necks of all powers must be bowed beneath the authority of the divine Scriptures; and, as the divine Jerome says, one must never flatter a human being in such a way that the truth of the holy Scriptures is neglected, which, throughout both Testaments, is true in the narration of deeds, right in admonitions, certain in promises, and terribly to be feared in threats.

For this reason it has not been given to all to be able to penetrate the mysteries of the divine Scriptures, but it is permitted only to those to whom love both continues study and the Spirit of God grants true understanding in purified minds. But whoever is filthy with the darkness of vices, whoever walks with a swollen mind proud: whoever doubts the truth of the Scriptures of God, whether in part or in whole, should never trust that he can arrive at an understanding of them. For the authority of Scripture itself says that unless you believe, you will not understand. It is the slowness of our intellect, and likewise the impurity of our desire, whenever we do not rightly understand the divine Scriptures: namely, when the veil of harmful preoccupation remains spread over our hearts, which does not permit us to come to true understanding. Hence it happens that we do not understand the sense which the Spirit has infused into the divine Scriptures, but, grasping the bare words of the writers, twist them into another sense. Indeed, if our minds were purified of carnal vices; if the intellect were exercised in the Scriptures through continual pursuit of sobriety; if that belief and reverence were applied to the holy Scriptures which their dignity requires, every diligent person would understand more clearly than daylight that there is nothing confused in the sacred readings, nothing discordant, nothing unsuitable, nothing absurd, or introduced without the most just reason. For all the passages of divine Scripture are full of mysteries; whenever something in them seems to have been placed obscurely, it has been done by divine providence, so that the diligent mind may have the necessary exercise of piety, and the faith of the simple may not lose the place of due reverence. Therefore it was not by chance, but by eternal providence, that he willed the holy Scriptures to be obscure in many places, so that they might abound in as many mysteries as senses in which, by the inspiration of the Spirit of God, they are expounded in Catholic fashion by the doctors. For, as holy Augustine says, the obscurity of divine Scripture is useful and very profitable, because it begets many judgments of truth and brings them forth into the light for human beings; for when one person, and another another, draws out this sense or that by expounding it in Catholic fashion, how lofty and profound it is becomes known.
