Hence let no man puffed up with secular learning suppose that he understands sacred Scripture unless he first lays aside the veil of pride and of every disordered concupiscence.

For secular learning is of greater value for exercising the intellect than for illuminating the understanding toward true wisdom. Therefore, without doubt, divine Scripture is both manifest and clear to minds purified through the continual exercise of the fear of God and frequent study in reading; to minds that are filthy and swollen with secular wisdom it seems confused and obscure. Hence he understands the holy Scriptures well and rightly who, with purified affection and frequent in their study, expounds them just as he did who wrote them. For if they are read in a spirit other than that by which he is believed to have inspired them to be written, the mind must necessarily be shut off altogether from true understanding. But when we encounter some discordance in them, let us understand that it is only of words, not of senses; and this arises in ordered fashion, not by chance, but by the providence of God, so that the mind, exercised longer in the Scriptures lest it become wholly sluggish, may be strengthened. For the counsel of God cannot be deceived; but the divine Scriptures were written by the counsel of his will; it follows necessarily that they are true and in no way false. They were human beings by whom the divine writings were handed down to us; certainly they wrote words used according to human custom, by which they might signify to posterity what that highest excellence of divinity willed to be known to mortals. Therefore now, you who, devoted to secular wisdom, attack the divine Scriptures, say: the Scripture of the New and Old Testament, which the Church has received and venerates as the true, authoritative, and holy Scripture of Christians, from where do you believe it was received? From God, or from human beings? If from God, why do you not believe it? For everyone who attacks Scripture which he believes to have been inspired by God most plainly resists the divine ordinance. But if it is from human beings, why do you hope for the eternal salvation promised in it, which man cannot give? Unless perhaps, madmen, you go on to say that all things are inventions, and that nothing that nothing remains after death and ashes, and that the mind together with the body passes into destruction, a profession that would show you to be no less mad than foolish. For if you truly believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, you will necessarily say that the divine Scriptures were inspired by the Holy Spirit. But if, having joined the apostates in a reprobate mind, you say that they were fabricated by men, you impiously show how far you are from true wisdom, wandering in darkness. You plainly show yourselves to be ignorant and rash judges, since you condemn Scripture, which you do not understand. But because it is more familiar to you to despise wisdom than to learn it, it is not the business of this work to weary the mind any longer against the rashness of the ignorant. This one thing I want you to know: that no one understands unless he receives; but because you interpose the filth of your affections so that you may not receive, for that reason understanding of true wisdom is not possessed.

For God, the illuminator of all, deigns by grace to be present to those who, stripped of carnal desires, burn with the fire of inward love, who desire nothing in this world except God. To them the Spirit of God brings help by his presence; those whom he has found rooted in the love of truth and purged of every extraneous thing he leads into the knowledge of all things. For truly, to those who love God, all things are open, all things naked, all things manifest, since whoever through love beholds in the faith of Jesus Christ the one who creates and governs all things knows all that is necessary for his salvation. But, on the other hand, the illumination of God dwells very far from the slothful, wicked feasters, the envious, the greedy, incubi, the filthy, the lustful, murderers, the impious, the proud, and those alien to piety; it leaves them to the judgment of the avenging demon, who, driving in the sharp point of savage fire, afflicts the senses and the mind, and all the more arms and drives the impious to commit crimes, so that, guilty of a more shameful fault, they may also become liable to a more bitter punishment. Hence, entangled in worldly vices and desires, they are not only unable to penetrate the divine Scriptures with understanding, but, neglecting themselves, they do not even know themselves.

Since, therefore, sacred Scripture is the perfect work of God, Caesar, we must so establish the mind that we believe it to be true, right, complete, solid, divinely inspired, and most abundantly sufficient for all who understand it for the confirmation of the Christian faith. For indeed, unless divine Scripture is believed to be true, holy, perfect in all things, and complete, the Christian faith would be deprived of its foundation. Therefore every Christian must take the greatest care not to overstep the bounds of piety by examining the divine Scriptures more than is fitting, because the author of the Scriptures is not man but the Holy Spirit; whoever struggles against the integrity of the Scriptures of God is proved to resist his ordinance. Scripture, moreover, by God’s ordering, is usefully interwoven in its figurative text with parables, enigmas, likenesses, and comparisons, so that readers may be exercised toward understanding, and, once its inward sweetness has been tasted, the mind may be strengthened toward piety.

And so, if with purified minds we attend to the sense of the Scriptures, not the words, we shall understand how rightly and properly all things have been ordered. For it was not fitting that the sacred Scriptures, in which knowledge of the divine majesty is handed down, should be so plain and manifest that they could be understood everywhere by all; for this knowledge is set forth to be understood only by the good and holy, not also by evil, filthy, and polluted minds. Hence it is written: “The beast that touches the mountain shall be overwhelmed with stones.” What is designated here by the beast, if not human beings who, in imitation of brutes, live without the love of God in the pleasures of the flesh? And what is expressed by the mountain, if not the height of the divine Scriptures? When the beast approaches this holy mountain, it is overwhelmed with stones, because a man impure in mind and weak in faith, who strives to search out the height of the divine Scriptures without a master to teach him, is struck down by various and pernicious errors, as though by stones.

is wounded by blows as though by stones. For just as all things are clean to the clean, so all things seem profane to the profane. God therefore placed his hiding place in the height of the Scriptures, which is so inaccessible and closed to the reprobate that it nevertheless always lies plainly open to the saints.

But why God did not make Holy Scripture sufficient and plain for all things that concern the Christian faith, we shall answer briefly. There are two things which the Most High provided for believers for the confirmation of the Christian faith: namely, the Church and Scripture, so that what is not expressed clearly enough in the one may be more fully declared by the other. Hence, if we find anything in the Holy Scriptures concerning the rules of faith expressed less sufficiently, we at once have recourse to the Church; and where the Church has need of saving instruction for piety, it immediately turns to Scripture. From this it follows that neither would the Church have authority without Scripture, nor Scripture credibility without the Church, so that the judgment of the two may be one. For Augustine says: I would not believe the Gospel unless the authority of the Church compelled me. But John Gerson says: I would not believe the Church unless the Gospel compelled me. Thus the Church confirms Holy Scripture, and is itself confirmed in like manner by Scripture. The Church supplies whenever Scripture is lacking; and if at any time the Church is in doubt, it has recourse to the counsel of Scripture. For there is one Holy Spirit of God, who founded the Church in the faith of Jesus Christ; the very same Almighty one alone inspired Scripture. And this is the threefold cord that is not easily broken: where divine Scripture is joined through the Holy Spirit to the authority of the Church, to such a degree that the Church commends Scripture, and Scripture in turn commends the Church. Therefore, O Caesar of unconquered majesty, as it seems to me, we have assigned a sufficient cause for the proposed question: since, if all things in the Holy Scriptures that concern the piety of faith were plainly expressed, holy mother Church would not seem to be of such great authority, and the merit of saving obedience would in large part be emptied out.

At the same time I think sufficient answer has been given to the principal question, where certain persons suppose Holy Scripture in very many places to be confused and imperfect; yet if they read it with due purity of mind, they would certainly find it perfect and sound. Great is the authority of the Catholic Church, which alone, in doubtful matters concerning the faith, has the right to interpret the Scriptures; to it the necks of all powers must be subjected. If anyone, with rash daring, has departed from its definition, he has denied the Gospel of Christ. There is one congregation of the faithful, the holy Church, mother of Christians, outside whose unity no one will be saved; and even if it sometimes appears weak in morals, nevertheless, always constant in faith, it has never erred, while the loving-kindness of Christ remains intact.

Question Five — Concerning the Reprobate

Hence no one among mortals is good unless, by the counsel of his own will, he is aided by the grace of the merciful God; and no one is evil unless, of his own accord, he is deprived of grace because of the obstacle of sin. By uprightness of will, however, we are made like the good spirits, if we prove the piety of the faith that we have in Christ by holy and necessary works. And just as the consummation of a good will makes good men equal to angelic spirits, so the perversity of the impious renders them like demons. Hence evil and perverse men, the more they have been depraved by the malice of their own will, the more they become like demons in disposition.

But likeness introduces the familiarity of friendship, from which mutual confidence is gradually generated. From the confidence of the lesser toward the greater there arises command, whether true or feigned by cunning. Thus if any command of depraved men over demons appears to exist, it arises from the greatness of depravity: namely, when their disposition is depraved to such a degree that, by a reprobate will, they either surpass or equal the malice of the demons who join themselves to them. For demons are not all equal in malice or intelligence; rather, one is much more cunning than another in quickness of understanding, and far worse in depraved affection. For those who, falling from the high seats, inhabit the hollows and caves of the earth are certainly duller than the rest, to such a degree that they fear swords and rods and seem to be admonished by the threats of men who terrify them, as can be observed in those whom we call energumens. But demons who dwell farther removed from the earth are subtler in nature and meet with men more rarely.

Men full of malice, however, the more they have advanced in perversity of will, the more they become like demons; and once admitted by them into familiarity, they thereafter become bold and receive command over the demons whose familiarity they use, not by violent power but by feigned pretense. For demons, in order to keep in their depravity those men whom they have once received into surrender as willing subjects, gladly submit themselves to them as though moved by a simulated dominion; and what they do voluntarily, they pretend they are compelled to do in obedience. For no one obtains true command over demons except him whom faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, through the merit of holiness, has made acceptable and a friend to God. For thus Scripture says of those who truly believe in the Lord Jesus: “And he gave them power over all demons.”

Evil men, therefore, command demons, whom malevolence has made like to them, likeness has made familiar, and familiarity has made their own and subject. It is as if some servant of a great prince, born in a humble station, as often happens, and joined to him by long familiarity, were said to command him, since he obtains from him without contradiction everything he asks, so that he himself seems rather to rule his lord than to be ruled by him. According to this likeness, evil and reprobate men, because they are admitted into the demons’ familiarity and become very bold through more prolonged confidence, receive over them a simulated, not to say familiar, command, which they have deserved by the likeness of their most depraved will. Hence whatever they have demanded from demons who join with them by an implicit or explicit compact, they receive, unless at times, being forbidden by divine ordinance, the demons cannot provide what is sought. Yet they do not thus join themselves indiscriminately to all reprobate and evil persons, but only to those with whom, through the intervention of a compact, they have entered into certain agreements: such as women who are witches, who have rendered homage to the devil, and those invokers of demons whom the common people call by the usual word necromancers.

¶ There are two kinds of men who can lawfully command demons.

¶ The first, indeed, is of those men who, beloved by God by the merit of holiness, have received from him the power of trampling the head of the ancient serpent, such as the apostles and their followers and disciples were in the primitive Church; concerning them the Lord speaks in the holy Gospel: “In my name they shall cast out demons,” and “They shall take up serpents.”

¶ The second kind is of those men to whom, by reason of order in the Church of God, it is granted that they may, by the power of the ministry received, drive demons out of human bodies. And this ministry is entrusted to exorcists in the Church of God when, that is, they are ordained by apostolic authority.

¶ Again, there are two kinds of men who desire to command demons; and the fact that they presume to do this unlawfully is shown by their most wicked conditions.

¶ The first kind, most pernicious, is of witches who enter into pacts with demons and, after a solemn profession has first been made, hand themselves over to some demon under the right of ownership and perpetual service. What great evils this most harmful kind of people commits in your empire, most wise Caesar, no one can express. For, first of all, denying God, the faith of Christ, and sacred baptism, they offer themselves in mind and body to demons; they weaken, injure, and kill men and beasts by their malefices. There is no disease that, God permitting, they cannot bring on, because when they present themselves to demons as servants in the observance of the contracted agreement, they dare whatever they wish in association with them. Hence they are nowhere to be tolerated, but rather are to be utterly exterminated in every place, as God, the creator of all, commands: “You shall not suffer witches to live.” Some witches summon demons by charms; others entice them by prayers and sacrifices; the rest, provoking them by unspeakable things and ceremonies, draw them into the aid of their impiety. It is therefore no wonder that witches seem to command demons, since by the impiety of a perverse will they have been made like them, and by mutual agreement familiar and subject to them.

¶ The second kind of depraved men who wish to command demons is of those ...those whom we commonly call necromancers. They profess arts full of execrations, by which they promise that they can summon demons into a circle, or show them openly and visibly enclosed in a crystal or some other vessel. These most pernicious men, full of falsehood and superstitions, commit such great evils as no good man could imagine. For in order to entice demons into obedience to themselves, they very often use the foulest sacrifices and enter into an explicit pact with them. They carry about many various little books full of filth, impiety, and falsehood, falsely inscribed with the names of ancient philosophers and sages; by displaying these they deceive many unwary and curious people and draw them with themselves into the demons’ pit. They promise great and utterly incredible things, the hearing of which keeps men suspended in wonder at the falsehood. By rings, pentacles, images, exorcisms, and conjurations, they say that they can constrain malignant demons so that they appear visibly in a circle, or in a crystal, or in some other receptacle, and answer distinctly to all questions asked. All indeed promise this, but in our times very few are found whom the malignant spirits obey in this way, even in evil matters, since God, for a most just reason, does not permit it: lest human curiosity, prone to novelties, after despising the religion of Christ, should in necessity seek help from demons. But all those whom malignant spirits, summoned by the conjurations of necromancers, obey have without doubt passed into fellowship with them by an explicit or implicit pact. Yet the number of the rest is greater: those whom the malignant spirits disdain to obey, although they do not fear to occupy themselves always in profane necromantic arts. And because especially in our times iniquity has begun to abound and charity has grown cold in many, these accursed and most deceitful men have grown too strong; and although they are despised by demons, nevertheless, persevering in their most pernicious doctrines, they deceive many.

Believe me, Caesar, this most deceitful kind of men is very pernicious to your sacred empire, and therefore, no less than the brood of witches, must be utterly exterminated. They promise great things and lie in everything. Indeed, all the things promised in their books are empty and false, and they furnish believers with nothing other than tricks, frauds, and the most subtle deceptions. And if at times they seem to produce what they have promised, it is manifest to everyone that this happens only by the cooperation of demons; fellowship with them must be fled no less than the most savage torments of hell. For demons very often come to these necromantic operations, and, so that they may keep their invokers obstinate in the treachery they have begun, they grant them, if they can, the things asked. Sometimes, however, when invoked by conjurations, they disdain to appear, and nevertheless they have carried away the minds of those who invoke them.

There is also another kind of men, no less foolish than superstitious: namely those who do not wish to have any commerce with demons, and yet use in their vain operations things appropriated to demons and therefore utterly illicit. For they think that great and hidden power resides in characters, and so they commit various errors against the faith of Christ. But because this is not the time to recount their madness, let us pursue our proposed subject. Why good and just men do not obtain command over demons must be stated briefly. Just as likeness of wills makes evil and impious men equal to demons, so unlikeness of wills renders good and just men wholly contrary to them. But among things contrary and unlike there can be no familiarity; rather, continual opposition and hatred are found. Where, however, no familiarity contracted by likeness of wills is found, neither can there be confidence of one toward the other, nor any mutual concurrence in the working of wonders. Nor should you, Caesar, boastNor do you, Caesar, glorious man, since you are a great ruler and prince of men, admit as familiar to you anyone whose character is altogether contrary and unlike to yours, and who continually resists your will. But good and upright men, because they always withstand the most depraved will of demons, can in no way pass over into fellowship with them; they neither wish nor consent to be familiar with them, but with all their strength flee from and detest meeting them. And therefore they do not obtain that fictitious command over them of which we have spoken. For nowhere is there secure familiarity where no likeness of wills has preceded it, nor can there be concord among opposites.

Yet demons do not obey all evil and reprobate persons indiscriminately, but only those with whom they are joined by pacts and services. And when invoked they willingly come to those whom they cannot otherwise keep faithful, although they lie that they are compelled. It is therefore not to be wondered at, most excellent Caesar, that malignant spirits sometimes seem to comply with depraved and perverse men, whom, as we have said, both malevolence and destructiveness toward the human race have made alike and concordant. But let it be far from every Christian to wish, through a depraved likeness of will, to command demons, because if anyone in this life begins to have fellowship with malignant spirits, in the life to come he will burn with them without end.

But why are good and just men unable to command the holy angels of God, into whose likeness of good will they have passed? I think the solution to this question could easily be given from what has been said above, if the difference of intellects is recalled to mind. For although there are many men established in the Church of God whose righteousness benefits many unto salvation, nevertheless in our times very few advance so far that, because of the merit of sanctity, they are either feared by demons or received by angels into the fellowship of familiarity. Hence it happens that the men of our age neither command malignant spirits by the merit of sanctity, nor deserve to be familiar with the holy angels. But if any have advanced to that degree of sanctity by which, performing miracles in the Church, the saints once advanced, then they can powerfully command demons and have familiar fellowship with the blessed spirits. For it is certain that holy men beloved by God, in the primitive Church of Christians, once bestowed greater benefits upon mortals through the cooperation of good spirits than the impiety of depraved men could ever have inflicted as evil deeds through the ministry of demons. For whoever is a true worshipper of God and has become like the holy angels can do many wondrous things by prayers.

ON THE POWER

Question Six — On the Power of Witches

The question of your most unconquered majesty was this: whence comes this so great power in witches, by which they can accomplish so many varied and wondrous things, even in a single hour, such things and so many as no good person could do in his whole life? To this question, if we wish to answer briefly, we must necessarily say that all power is from the Lord God, without whom no creature can do anything. For Christ says in the holy Gospel: Without me you can do nothing. Hence it is manifest that every power of doing anything is granted to human beings by the Lord God and from no other source, whether they do good or evil.

Hence the most holy prelate Augustine says: The will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily appearances and motions; and nothing happens in this most vast and immense commonwealth of the whole creature, visibly, which is not either commanded or permitted from the inner, invisible, and intelligible court of the supreme emperor, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments. Therefore, Caesar, there is no doubt that that power of witches, by which they produce wondrous and horrible effects through the cooperation of demons, comes from the Lord God. is granted by the Lord God, whose will no one can resist, and without whose influence a man cannot even move his hand. For the holy doctors conclude that neither demons nor witches can do anything, whether to harm a person or an animal, unless God himself wills it, consents, and grants the power, so that they may do what they have already resolved upon with a perverse will. Unless God consents and wills, no creature can do anything; otherwise, if anything could happen when he did not will and consent to it, it would necessarily follow that God was weak, since he could not prevent what, though unconquered, he would be forced to permit to happen.

But since every human being, insofar as he is a creature, depends on God, he can do nothing without the will of him from whom he has both the will and the power. Whatever, therefore, witches do is done with God permitting it; without his will they can do nothing, because unless God has granted it, they will obtain neither from themselves nor from demons the ability to do what they wish. And so all power is from the Lord God, in whom all things exist and are moved as in the first cause of all things; for from him from whom we received freedom of choice, from him also we have the power to do what we will.

But since the understanding of witches is very confused, they perpetrate the evils they do not by human art, but by the cooperation of demons, whom nature has made subtle and long experience has made swift in producing wonders. For the effects of witches are not caused by such means as they use for witchcraft, such as heads of the dead, toads, serpents, characters, images, and things similar to these, but by the devil who established these signs; since he is most proud, he desires in all things to be seen as comparable to God. For just as God once instituted certain sacraments in his Church, which, when worthily administered and with him assisting, signify and produce a saving effect, while he himself who instituted them works salvation, so also the devil, who desires nothing more than to be regarded as equal to God, instituted certain signs as if they were sacraments. When he is invoked by them by those to whom he is allied by covenants and pacts, the malignant operator assists; and as often as God has permitted it, he effects the evil that is asked. If God has not permitted it, he does absolutely nothing. For indeed, of all the effects of necromancers and witches the devil is the operator; by the application of the means which he himself first established to the subject matter, he produces the desired work, sometimes really, sometimes only apparently.

But women witches, who by now, with a depraved will and consent, have passed into fellowship with demons through pacts, receive from them certain marks and symbolic signs, by which, when summoned, the demons immediately come. Nothing in these destructive operations of demons is stronger than the foolish credulity of witches, which is increased by pacts and vows, since the firmer the faith they have placed either in the demons or in their signs, the swifter the operation they attain with the demons cooperating. For the excessively savage depravity of the witches’ will in a certain way turns them into madness; when this has preoccupied the mind, the demons at once apply themselves to those who are raving, and, invited by pacts and signs, with God permitting it, they supply the effect of the petition to the women in their frenzy.

For Plato related something similar in the book On Poetic Frenzy, saying: just as bacchant women, when of unsound mind, draw honey and milk from rivers, but when of sound mind they cannot draw them. Their spirit, carried outside itself into fellowship with an evil demon, effects this. We know by experience that witches at times have drawn butter from rushing rivers, which can in no way happen except by the ministry of a demon. In a similar way, when they have been brought into hatred of some person or animal, and sigh for its destruction, they are driven by a most grievous fury, thinking of nothing in their mind except revenge. They take up the things known and familiar to them for witchcraft, invoke demons, and show the signs established by them together with the characters; and what they cannot accomplish by their own power, they obtain by the demons’ ministry.

But another person, who is not subject to demons by pact and surrender, even if he knows the things suitable for witchcraft together with the method of operation, and although he displays the signs, nevertheless rarely achieves the effect the effect, because he is not counted among the familiar associates of demons. For the devil, puffed up with pride, imitates the church of Christ to such a degree that, just as one who has not been ordained cannot consecrate the body of Christ, however much he may utter the words of consecration, so too a demon, however much he may be invoked and however much signs or characters may be shown to him, either never or only rarely comes to the aid of someone whom he does not know to be subject to him by pact. For if he came indiscriminately to all who invoked him, without pacts having been interposed, he would not possess so many witches dedicated to him by right of ownership.

Hence it is that many who are given over to profane arts, laboring with dreadful conjurations to summon demons to a circle, to a mirror, or to any other receptacles, obtain no effect, because either the command of God stands in the way, or the devil despises the curious man who has not been dedicated to him by homage. For three things are required for witchcraft, without which it is agreed that none is perpetrated: a witch raging in mind and with depraved will; also the cooperation of a familiar demon; and, before all things, divine permission. But if one of these does not concur, the witchcraft cannot be perpetrated. For if God did not permit it, neither the devil nor the witch could do anything. And if the devil did not come to the aid of the wicked woman’s will, she would perpetrate no witchcraft. Again, if the witch were lacking, the devil would in no way complete the witchcraft. For the devil uses the will of the raging witch as an artisan uses an instrument for working; without it he could not inflict the witchcraft.

And just as demons differ from one another in power and in the sharpness of their subtlety, so the power of witches is not one and the same in all of them, but differs in individuals according as demons of subtler or grosser nature come together with them. For there are many kinds of demons, and they are separated from one another by fixed degrees, by reason of the places into which, when they fell at the beginning, they were thrust down. The first kind of demons indeed is called fiery, because it wanders about the upper air and is never plunged down to the lower regions before the day of judgment; rather, remaining continually beneath the lunar regions, they have no commerce with human beings on earth. That they remain beneath the moon, Saint Augustine testifies in the work On the Christian Struggle, saying as follows: Demons do not dwell in heaven, where the sun and stars are, but all pass their time beneath the lunar region.

Moved by this, as I think, Apuleius said that demons are fiery animals, because Aristotle confirmed that in burning furnaces certain small animals have often been seen flying about, furnished with little wings, which spend their whole life in fire, since they arise with the fire and are extinguished with it, and, vanishing, return to their own place from which they had come. They have no association with acts of witchcraft, because, since they dwell in fire, on account of their subtlety they cannot take on a gross or airy body.

The second kind is called aerial, because it wanders in the air and dwells near us. These, indeed, can descend to the lower regions, and, with bodies assumed from denser air, sometimes appear visibly to human beings. God permitting, they often disturb the air; they stir up thunder and storms; and all together they conspire for the ruin of the human race. In the manner of human beings they are moved by the affections of passions, especially pride and envy, and they are driven by continual disturbances; they are not clothed with a solid body, nor do they remain in one place. Nor do they all have one form, but many, and they often change them according to the variety of the affections by which they either come when summoned by the spells of witches, or are driven by disturbance to do harm. For they have an altogether violent and furious disposition, full of disturbances; hence, when strongly wronged and disturbed, they very often contrive sudden ambushes. While they make their incursions, they partly wish to remain hidden, and partly inflict violence. Witches of these demons Witches, supported by the cooperation of these demons, are more powerful in doing harm in proportion as they have obtained the concurrence of one higher in their order. In the Life of Saint Anthony, Saint Athanasius said that the air is full of demons; Mercury, the Thrice-Greatest, had also said this earlier, namely that no part of the world is without the presence of demons. The holy bishop Ambrose also says: The world is full of holy powers because it is full of wickednesses. Hence the Platonists have handed down that demons flying in the air, like very dense fiery snow, are visible to those who desire it, if for some time, while the sun is shining, they keep their gaze directed toward heaven with eyes not beaten back. But I do not know whether the object in the air is caused by a real consistency, or whether the interrupted motion of the eyes presents false images; nevertheless, not without slight damage to the sense, I have made trial of the things promised.

The third kind, however, we call terrestrial demons; we do not in the least doubt that they fell from heaven to earth according to their deserts. Concerning these, the most holy bishop and martyr of Christ, Theophorus, once called Ignatius, wrote thus in a certain letter to the Ephesians: There is nothing better than to have peace, in which every weapon of the aerial and likewise the terrestrial spirits is made void. Of these demons, some move about in forests and groves, laying ambushes for hunters; others live in open fields and make travelers wander at night; some dwell in hidden places and caves; the rest, less frenzied and disturbed than the others, delight to dwell with human beings in the dark. They are not led by one affection but by various ones, since some are less depraved than others, although all are full of evil disturbances. Of these, some rejoice in terrifying human beings by illusions alone; others desire to draw their hearers into admiration of themselves by predictions of future things. Some, however, labor with this whole effort: that they may terrify, injure, or kill human beings disturbed by irrational frenzy or raging with melancholy, as we have learned by experience has often happened. Hence Saint John Chrysostom, in the third book On Providence to the monk Stagirius, says: In every diabolical action, the magnitude of grief is more powerful for doing harm, because whomever a demon overcomes, he overcomes through grief. If you take that away, no one will be able to be harmed by a demon. This kind of demons, however, is rarely familiar to witches, because of the inconstancy of their affections and the levity by which they delight more in terrifying many people than in being subject to the command of one little woman. Yet sometimes, as they promise to madwomen, they dwell in glass, or in crystal, or in a mirror, and, when stirred up by incantations, they give answers to women; and if someone coming on the road has spoken ill of them, they announce it beforehand. And this kind of witches sometimes differs greatly from the rest, since what the others make infirm by sorcery, these women promise to cure. But because for the most part they repel sorcery by sorcery, every Christian is forbidden by the Church to have recourse to them.

The fourth kind of demons is called aquatic, because, immersing itself in waters, it dwells around lakes and rivers: full of wrath, disturbed, restless, and deceitful. It stirs up storms at sea, sinks ships into the deep, and takes the lives of many in the waters. And whenever these demons assume a visible body, they more often appear in the female sex, and are seen more rarely in the male, because they move about in damp places and follow a softer course of life, nor can they easily assume a lowly form according to the custom of the others. Long ago antiquity named the Naiads and Nereids, nymphs of the waters, not in the male sex but in the female. But others are commonly called aquatic women, that is, wasser frawen. Those who live in drier, somewhat arid places, whenever they appear bodily visible to human beings, transform themselves into men. They also assume the forms of various They assume the forms of beasts according as they are touched by various affections. But the holy angels, since they are never altered by affection, always appear uniformly in male form. For nowhere do we read it written that a good spirit was seen in the form of a woman or of any beast, but always in male appearance. Demons, however, have rather often been seen around rivers and springs in the appearance of women: sometimes dancing, sometimes letting down their hair in the manner of a woman, and sometimes speaking with human beings and carrying out various mockeries. And this kind of demons has not customarily had commerce with witches.

The fifth kind is called subterranean, because it dwells in caves and caverns and in the remote hollows of mountains. And these demons are very evil in disposition. They especially attack those who dig wells and mines, and those who seek treasures hidden in the earth, being most ready for the destruction of the human race. They make openings in the earth, stir up flame-vomiting winds, and shake the foundations of buildings. Sometimes at night, coming out of the mountains in troops, they lead marvelous and astonishing dances in the fields, as though fearing the command of a single leader. At a sign they suddenly vanish and return to their hiding places. At times the sound of bells is heard among them, and sometimes they falsely claim that they are the spirits of men departed from life. They seek nothing more than the fear and wonder of human beings. Hence we have found that they have sometimes led certain simpler people into their hiding places in the mountains, showing astonishing spectacles to those who marveled, and they falsely claim that dwellings of the blessed are there, and that they are friends of the living.

Among these demons, too, some are brooding guardians of treasures, which the avarice of mortals has hidden in the earth; and lest they come again into human use, they remove them, steal them, guard them, and sometimes transfer them from place to place. And this kind of demons has not customarily had any commerce with witch-women.

The sixth kind of demons is called light-fleeing, because they especially abhor and detest light: for they never appear by day, nor can they assume a body in any other way than at night. This is the business that walks about in darkness: a kind of demons that is inscrutable and utterly dark, agitated by cold passions, malicious, restless, and disturbed, which violently oppresses people it encounters in the night hours. Rather often, God permitting, it kills certain people either by its breath or by its touch. This kind of demons does not associate with witches, nor can it be constrained by charms, because it flees both light and human voices, and every disturbance as well.

The aerial kind is especially accustomed to attend the sorceries of women, since it is more subtle than all the others and of the most audacious rashness. Some of the terrestrial demons also, as has been said, serve witches; yet because they are held in a lower rank, they are by no means able to bring about those greater sorceries. It is therefore plainly established that the whole power of witches, by which they do such wondrous things, is granted to demons by the Lord God within limits; and when he does not permit it, they accomplish nothing.

ON DIVINE PERMISSION. Seventh Question.

Question Seventh

The seventh question of your most serene majesty was this: Why does almighty God, since he is just and the avenger of evils, permit such great sorceries to be done for the destruction of the human race, by which not only sinners but also many innocent people perish, grievously tormented?

To this question, I remember that I answered in this way some time ago, when I had been placed before your majesty. Almighty God is just and upright, kind and merciful. Whatever he permits, he permits justly, because he is just, and there is no iniquity with him; rather, he permits all things that happen in true judgment. Therefore, when it is asked why God permits evil things to be done, we answer: He permits them for this reason: because he is just. Let the answer we have given not seem absurd to your majesty, O Caesar, since it in no way prejudices divine goodness that he permits evils to be done for a most just reason; rather, indeed, it would prejudice it if he did not permit evils to be done in the present world. For truly, if he did not permit evils to be done, man would now be unable to sin; he would certainly be impeccable, which does not belong to his nature, to which the Creator of all gave free will from the beginning. For since man is a creature and not the Creator, he is necessarily capable of being turned toward good as well as toward evil; his being depends on the supreme maker of all creatures, just as every caused thing depends on the cause of its own being. But to create has been left to God alone, who is incorruptible and everlasting; everything corruptible, however, necessarily fails, but is preserved by the goodness of the Creator so long as it does not lose the influence of its cause. Hence it neither could nor ought to have happened that man should be created impeccable by the condition of his nature, a thing that only God, the maker of all, naturally enjoys, who is immutable and everlasting. Whenever, indeed, it is granted to man that he seems unable to sin, freedom of choice is not removed, nor is the possibility simply taken away, but the will is confirmed in good. And whenever this gift is conferred on a creature, it is a gift of grace, not of nature. For Scripture says: God from the beginning created man and left him in the hand of his own counsel. For, properly speaking, it cannot be that mortal man, conceived in original displeasure, should both have free will and be unable to commit sin. For the most holy bishop Augustine says: The first freedom of the will was to be able to sin; the last, in glory, will much more be to be unable to sin. Therefore, if man could not sin, he would not have mastery over his own will. Hence, although almighty God does not will sin, yet he justly permits men to sin and to do evil, so that, while freedom of choice remains, both the virtue of a good work may receive its reward, and voluntary depravity may receive the evil it has done. For no one either does good or sins unwillingly. Therefore almighty God justly permits men to sin and to do evil, since he granted them freedom of choice from the beginning. There are, moreover, many reasons long ago assigned by the holy doctors why the Almighty permits such great sorceries to be done through the cooperation of demons; of these we shall necessarily make brief mention in order.

The first is so that the excellence of divine power may be made manifest, for he alone is immutable and above every ordinance of law. Every mutable creature has no comparison with the immutable Creator. Hence in Numbers we read: God is not like a man, that he should lie, nor like a son of man, that he should be changed. In Isaiah also it is said: God is faithful, without iniquity, just and upright. In the book of Tobit it is also written: You are just, O Lord, and all your judgments are true, and all your ways are mercy, truth, and judgment. And in the book of holy Job we read: Impiety is far from God, and iniquity from the Almighty. For he will render to a man his work, and according to the ways of each he will restore to them. Therefore every man who rightly understands his own ignorance and weakness plainly recognizes how much he is nothing in comparison with his Creator. For God justly permits man to sin, both so that freedom of choice may be continued and so that the excellence of the great God may become known to human beings.

The second reason is so that the inscrutable wisdom of God may become known to mortals, since he knows how to draw good out of our evils, when he makes one person’s sin become another person’s merit for the increase of virtue. For if he did not permit evil to be done, which of us would understand good? For God makes and orders good; evils, however, he does not make, but he disposes that those done by the impious should not come about in a disordered way. Nor does the malice of men impede the will of God, nor can man do anything that God does not permit.

The third cause, indeed, is that the Almighty permits sorceries to be done so that he may manifest his most merciful goodness toward those who have sinned and done penance, which he could in no way show if he did not permit the creature to sin. For if there were no sinner, God could not be one who has mercy. But since we all offend in many things, everywhere God finds something to remit; everywhere the guilty person appears, in whom the kindly Creator may show his mercy. Hence the holy bishop Augustine: If the disease were slight, the physician would be despised and would not be sought; if the physician were not sought, the disease would not come to an end. Therefore where sin abounded, grace also abounded, which alone distinguishes the redeemed from the lost, whom the mass of perdition, drawn from the origin of creation, gathers into one. Therefore the mercy of the Lord is over all his works.

The fourth reason for divine permission is that the justice of the Creator may be declared toward those who have sinned and have not done penance, since if all did good and no one sinned, God’s justice would have nothing to punish. Therefore, so that justice may have a place, by divine permission the creature sins. For the Lord is just, who will render to each according to the work of his will.

The fifth reason is the dignity of the human condition: because if God did not permit man to sin, he would seem worse than brute beasts, which, with no violence driving them, freely use the motions of nature. For even if brute beasts lack reason, nevertheless they have a free motion of nature which they follow; in comparison with this, man would seem of a lower condition if he did not have free choice of the will. But God permitted free will to man, over which neither kings nor princes rule.

The sixth reason is the praise of the merit of steadfastness in human virtue, since we praise a just man for this reason: that although he could have transgressed, he did not transgress, but, with the grace of God assisting him, remained in the steadfastness of a good will.

The seventh reason why almighty God permits demons to do such great evil deeds through the agency of witches is that those who, scorning truth, delight in falsehood may, seduced by the devil, the inventor of falsehood, be utterly deceived.

For it is fitting that enchanters and witches, who despise the saving teachings of Christ, should all, deceived by demons, be plunged down to hell to be punished forever. They seek aid from demons, the enemies of the whole human race, and they despise the Savior of the world, whom alone they ought to have adored. For it is just that he who, deserting truth by his own spontaneous will, adheres to falsehood should be cast headlong by the devil into destruction.

The eighth cause is the manifestation of divine power, whose might and virtue are over every creature. Indeed, when almighty God sometimes permits great things to the devil and denies certain small things, it is apparent how weak the enemy of the human race is, and subject to the divine majesty in all things. Whatever he does, he does with God permitting it. Therefore the first cause of all, on account of which almighty God permits evil deeds to be done, is justice, by which he preserves in inviolable order the freedom that he once bestowed upon the creature from the beginning. But because the power of every creature, depending on its Creator, is restricted and limited, it is manifest that he does not wish the devil to be able to do everything, nor man, however depraved in will. The will indeed is free, but power is limited by fixed and necessary degrees. For if demons could do everything they wish, nothing in human affairs would remain safe, but they would overthrow everything.

The history of holy Job demonstrates by a manifest example the bound power of demons: Satan did not dare to tempt him beyond what had been permitted to him by divine dispensation. For no one in the present world, however just or strong, could resist the fury of demons if they were always able, according to their own choice, to use free power to do harm. But before the Lord’s passion they used a greater freedom of power than afterward; but when Christ tasted death for us on the altar of the cross, their power was thereafter greatly diminished, as the Savior says in the Gospel: Now the prince of the world “will be cast out.” For indeed Christ’s humility and the perseverance of the saints have greatly restrained the boldness of demons, so that they can rightly be called inciters of evils, but by no means compellers. Nor would the devil gain strength against us unless he received his strength from our sins. Hence Scripture admonishes us, saying, “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” And again, “Do not give place to the devil.”

Therefore, to bring the discussion to a conclusion for understanding the question proposed, why God permits so many acts of harmful magic to be done, I believe the reasons have been sufficiently made clear. For even if the will of demons is always wicked, their power can never be unjust, since what it wickedly wills it has from its own choice, but what it can wickedly do it has from God alone. And these things have been said insofar as they concern those who do evil.

But why does almighty God permit demons, through the agency of sorcerers, to harm people who have been baptized in the name of the holy Trinity and faithfully believe in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ? For if they could harm only the evil, the perverse, and unbelievers in body and goods, but were restrained from approaching and harming the good and faithful, the permission would rightly seem to be a just judgment. But now the good and innocent are more often made sick by the harmful magic of demons, and sometimes are even deprived of life, to pass over in silence the loss of temporal goods that those bewitched often suffer. Many are troubled as to why the Almighty permits these things, he who permits nothing unjustly.

For this proposed question, I shall set out in order, as briefly as I can, the necessary reasons, received from no others than the ancient and Catholic doctors. The first reason is the testing of Christians’ faith and the proving of their integrity: so that, when scourged by the harmful magic of demons, they may learn in the sufferings of the flesh what faith and love toward God they have hidden in the mind. In prosperity it is not difficult to be long-suffering; but in adversity, with humble patience, to await help from the Savior of the faithful is not the mark of the soft, but of the strong and of truly faithful Christians. In his tribulation most holy Job learned how great a constancy of faith toward God he possessed, he who before, in tranquility, had preserved his piety without the dart of temptation.

Here at the same time it must be noted that those whom the harmful magic of demons or men has in any way made sick, and who, in order to recover health, either approach or consult any sorcerers and enchanters, whether by themselves or through others, act against the precepts of God and the Church; and they have neither true faith in God nor love. For they prefer the health of mortal flesh to God, and seek salvation not from Christ but from the devil and his minister. They prefer to live healthy, but unhappily, in the name of the devil, rather than to suffer a little here for the love of Christ and afterward rejoice with him forever.

But one who does not approach sorcerers because God has forbidden it, preferring to live with observance of God’s commandments in poverty and sickness rather than against God in riches and bodily health, truly loves God and rightly preserves the integrity of the Christian faith.

Most sacred Caesar, people corrupt in mind and reprobate with respect to the faith must not be tolerated among Christians: those who cure the bewitched by harmful magic; those who reveal thefts and adulteries through the ministry of demons; those who foretell future things by inspecting stones or mirrors. I beg you, do not listen to those who, ignorant of the divine laws, think that ministers of demons of this kind are useful to your rule because they know how to dissolve acts of harmful magic by harmful magic. For that destructive cure of bodies brings about the death of souls, and makes men withdraw from God, the creator of all things, and adhere to impious apostate demons, with whom after death they will be damned forever.

The second reason why almighty God permits the innocent to be harmed by harmful magic is the increase of merits: namely, so that, once their patience has been proved in tribulation, they may merit a worthier crown of glory in heaven. For, as holy Augustine says, a man is unknown to himself as to what he can bear and what he cannot bear. Sometimes he fears that he cannot bear what nevertheless he can. When temptation comes, like a kind of interrogator, a man is discovered by himself, who before, being hidden, did not know himself. The holy arch-apostle Peter, before temptation came upon him, was hidden both from himself and from others, namely that he was heedless and weak; it came, and the weakness that had lain hidden appeared. Therefore temptation is the greatest proving of men, as sacred Scripture bears witness: the furnace proves the potter’s vessels, and the temptation of tribulation proves just men. Patience is easy in prosperity, when no adversity strikes the mind. But many are the tribulations of the just; yet from them all our Lord Jesus Christ will deliver them.

The third reason for divine permission is the preservation of humility, so that the faithful and just man may always fear God and never presume upon his own strength or justice. Hence Scripture says of the reprobate: They are not in the labor of men, and with men they will not be scourged. Therefore pride held them; they were covered with their iniquity and impiety; their iniquity came forth as if from fatness. It belongs to the mercy of God that he sometimes permits good and just men to be shaken by adversities, whom he knows cannot be humbled in prosperous circumstances. For tribulation has made many humble whom favorable circumstances would have made proud. Finally, the fearful imagining of malefices makes a good man fear his God and diligently call upon his aid. But let no one, proud and presuming upon his own powers, think himself safe from the malefices of demons; for the man whom the protection of God abandons, inflated with pride, without doubt lies open to the malefices of demons.

The fourth reason is so that there may be a distinction between the good and the evil. For Scripture says of good men, beloved by God, in the Acts of the Apostles, that through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God. And holy Paul, lover of Christ, says in a certain epistle: All who wish

H iij to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution. Likewise the wisest king Solomon says in Proverbs: Whom the Lord loves, he corrects, and, like a father, he is pleased with his son. It is a very glorious thing for a Christian, suffering for the love of God, to endure adversities, whether they are inflicted by evil men or by demons. For power is given to the devil and his ministers to harm good and just men, not for their destruction, as the inexperienced suppose, but rather for the very great and certain consolation of the soul.

Indeed, when a just man lives well, harms no one, offends no one, does injury to no one, loves his God with his whole heart, fears and venerates him, and keeps his commandments with all care, yet nonetheless is troubled by malefices, whether in body, in possessions, or in both, truly blessed is that man; for when he has been proved, he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him. Everyone who lives rightly in the unity of the faith of the catholic Church of Christians, and, receiving evils in this world, patiently endures them for the love of God, is a sure sign that he perseveres in the grace of God and is to be saved.

On the contrary, concerning the evil and reprobate we read it written thus: Why do the impious live? They have been raised up and strengthened with riches. Their houses are secure, and the rod of God is not upon them. They spend their days in good things, and in a moment they descend to hell. For it is a manifest sign of damnation if you live badly here in sins and vices, opposed to God, and yet prosper in the goods of fortune and in bodily health.

The fifth reason why the Almighty permits good and just men to be troubled by the evil and reprobate is for the complete purification of the mind. For, as Scripture says, there is no just man on earth who does good and does not sin. But since God lets no sin pass unpunished, he ordains temporal punishments for just men, through mercy, for their faults, but eternal punishments for the impious and reprobate, through justice. Therefore, out of mercy, he changes eternal punishment for the penitent into temporal punishment, which either in in this world, or after death in purgatory. But because the torments of purgatory are dreadful and very grave, the merciful God is accustomed to purify in this life, in various ways, the penitents whom he loves, through the hardships of diverse tribulations in body and in possessions.

For the evil works of the impious benefit good and just people as a remedy, but bring damnation upon those who inflict them. The sixth reason is that a person, harmed through the assaults of demons, may be recalled to penitence and may resolve in his heart on the necessary amendment of life. For Almighty God does not immediately send vengeance when we sin, but waits for our amendment until a predetermined time. But if we have neglected to do penance, the avenger of evils comes to us when we do not expect it; and we who, as sinners, have scorned to acknowledge ourselves by doing penance in tranquility, will at last acknowledge ourselves late, in tribulation. Hence the holy prophet speaks in the person of God, saying: If his sons abandon my law and do not walk in my judgments and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with blows; but my mercy I will not take away from them, nor will I do harm in my truth.

The seventh reason why Almighty God permits the evil works of demons to prevail over the good and innocent is that an excessively unrestrained occasion for sinning may be cut away from them. For there are many poor and sick people, pleasing to God, good, devout, and humble, whom poverty and bodily illness preserve in the love of God; if they were rich and raised high with honors, they would quickly fall away from the resolve of holiness into the depth of vices. It is not expedient for everyone’s salvation to have honors and riches together with health, nor does a longer life always make a person better. Therefore Almighty God, wishing to show his mercy toward those whom he has chosen, permits the good, the just, and the innocent to be subject to various calamities.

And sometimes through demons, sometimes through evil people, and sometimes through various other ways and means, he takes away from such people the riches and honors which he foreknew they would use badly, so that in poverty and abasement they may keep the humility which, placed in wealth and high station, they would by no means have preserved. He also often permits them to fall into many great illnesses, because cheerful bodily health would have brought upon them the greatest sickness of mind. Finally, he permits certain people to be driven to death by sorcery, so that the license for sinning may be cut away from them, which they would have abused for longer had they been allowed to remain in life. Hence Scripture says of the just man: He was snatched away lest malice change his understanding, and lest deceit deceive his soul.

The eighth reason for divine permission is that people may venerate the sacraments of the Church, which have a powerful virtue against all the evil works of malignant spirits. For a person who venerates the sacraments and rites of the catholic Church with due honor is rarely harmed by the evil works of demons. And by the very confession of witches we have often heard that attendance at masses and the use of things blessed by the Church greatly weaken the powers of demons. Nor are things blessed in the Church of God in vain, but so that they may be, as it were, defenses of divine protection and tokens to be feared by demons. But concerning children and infants who, reborn in Christ, are sometimes killed by the evil works of demons or of human beings, we do not doubt that divine providence permits this to happen for their salvation, since it knows how to order all things for the better for mortals. Yet it often happens that infants perish by sorcery because of the offenses of their parents.

ON THE PROVIDENCE OF GOD The Eighth Question.

Question Eighth

The eighth question of your Serenity was this: whether it can be proved by natural reason, as also from the Holy Scriptures, that God has care for human affairs and actions, and a sure and infallible providence over all and each of the things that are done in the world.

To this question I remember that I answered as follows. The whole world, heaven and earth and all things that are in them, are subject to divine providence; by its will and command they were brought forth into being from the beginning. For there is nothing in the whole universe that is not governed by the providence of the Creator. Let us confirm this opinion first by the Scriptures, and afterwards by reasons, as briefly as possible. In the book of Judith we read: “All your ways are peaceful, and you have placed all judgments in your providence.” And in Ecclesiastes the most wise king Solomon speaks thus: “Do not give your mouth so as to make your soul sin, nor say before the angel, ‘There is no providence,’ lest perhaps the Lord, angered against your words, destroy all the works of your hands.”

The most manifest testimonies of providence are confirmed in the holy Gospel, when our Savior says to the disciples: “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarius? And one of them does not fall to the ground before God?” This is a great commendation of divine providence, which has care not only for men but also for the smallest birds. Indeed, if the Almighty cares for such small things, who would not believe that he has care for great things? “Look,” he says, “at the birds of heaven, which neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.” And a little later he adds, saying: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is and tomorrow is cast into the oven, how much more you, of little faith?” Since God is almighty, because he created all things and brought them into being when they did not exist, he rules and governs the universe lest it fall and pass away. This could in no way happen if he did not have providence and care for all things. For if providence is removed, it is necessary that the order of continuity of the whole universe be thrown into confusion. But the providence of the Creator cares for all things, since he who feeds the birds, gives their food to the beasts of burden, fills every living creature with blessing, and clothes the grass of the field, adorning violets and lilies with beautiful grace, cannot forget man, whom from the beginning he created in his own image. He who governs all things cares for all things; and he carries out providence not only for man, but also for all beasts of burden. All things are placed under his dominion, and there is no one who can resist his will in anything.

Let us now, therefore, consider this vast structure of the whole universe: how it always perseveres, most orderly, in its original arrangement and motion. Unless we shamefully go astray in mind, we shall understand by the most manifest reason that the divine and unchangeable providence preserves, directs, and governs these things. Next let us contemplate all earthly things, each of which, most orderly, is born and proceeds in its own natural arrangement. This cannot happen by chance; rather, they must be moved by the will of him by whose power they were made and created.

Then, in turn, consider the earth placed in the middle of the world like a point or center, which unfolds the circle at an equal distance from the whole universe; nothing more beautiful, nothing more adorned, nothing finally more delightful to the sense could present itself as suitable. In this point of an immense mass, enclosed by that very mass, we discern all things wonderfully ordered, and nothing could be left unordered. Thus all things that sometimes seem to us somehow to float about, we may know for certain, do not lack their own particular order within the order of the universe. For by the simple and altogether unchangeable nod of God, the whole structure of the entire universe, composed of so many diverse and moving things, is ruled and harmonizes in the most orderly way. Certainly, in those things that present themselves to our senses, we see that, in any governor, the greater the intelligence and power that arise with time, the more he the less can anything disorderly happen by fortuitous chance. Since, therefore, that supreme intellect, the creator, preserver, and ruler of all things, almighty God, rules and governs the world by his unchangeable providence, holding all things under his command, surely no place anywhere is left for rash chance, which might impede the will of so great a majesty.

Therefore the universe, whatever exists anywhere or can exist, is comprehended under the rule of one divine mind, whose infallible judgment nothing can escape. But unexpected events happen to us because we are changeable and are changed almost daily, having no determinate knowledge of future things. But that best maker of all things, God, since he is altogether unchangeable, knows all things, beholds all things, and understands all things at once and simultaneously. His providence is not deceived; his will is never changed; his power is not broken; his ordering is not violated; his counsel is never interrupted, even if his decision sometimes seems to be changed. Hence, if we attend carefully, we shall plainly understand, as the ends of things and motions will show, that all these lower things are made, preserved, disposed, and moved by divine providence, to whose command nothing at all is alien. For God himself, the lord of the universe, understands both all things and each thing: not stretched out, after our fashion, among many things, but abiding in himself as an indivisible unity. By contemplating himself as the pattern of the whole universe, and the cause of causes, and through causes the cause of all things, he beholds all things; and in beholding, he cares for and provides for each thing, directing it to its end and good by an everlasting order.

Come now, most wise Caesar, so that we may understand divine providence governing all things, let us use arguments as briefly as we can for our purpose. Therefore, if God's action is his own understanding, which no wise man fails to admit as at once most eminent and most inward, then as much as he acts, so much surely he understands, and conversely. But he acts in individual things, not only in great things but even in the smallest; therefore he understands individual things. For the first Being has, through each and every being that follows in fixed orders, a most ample influence; and the things that act after him are everywhere moved and act by his power.

Either, then, God understands or does nothing outside himself, which is false; or, in acting upon all things and each thing, he also understands those same things, which is true. For they would never be made unless first, to speak in our fashion, they were understood by God himself, who makes them, just as things are not made by the sun unless they are looked upon by it. But because the omnipotent one understands all things and each thing that he makes, there is no doubt that he disposes, rules, and orders all things that he has made; and from him things have not only that they exist, but also that they are certain causes of other things. Thus, if things have from God that they are causes, from him also they have received the proper office of a cause, that is, to preserve according to their powers and to care for what they have made. Therefore, if all causes have this property from the first cause, insofar as they are certain causes, rightly does that first cause naturally have this goodness and providence, so that he cares for all things and each thing that he has made, insofar as he is most of all the cause of them all and of each of them.

Indeed, unless these things are guarded individually by him who makes them, the common things that are preserved in individual things will never be guarded. For the whole, which consists of parts, will not be preserved if the parts themselves are neglected. Therefore from the intention of the first and greatest common intelligence proceeds the universal distinction of things. This intelligence, however, is distinguished of itself from others, and by the standard of its own knowledge distinguishes the rest among themselves. Hence, just as God knows all things and each thing most distinctly, so also he most distinctly rules, moderates, and cares for them.

Therefore I think it is manifest, most clement Caesar Maximilian, and sufficiently shown, that the providence of God, the supreme ruler, embraces, disposes, rules, and moderates all lower things and each thing, which otherwise, without the provident disposition of one who observes them, would not continue this order which we perceive. they would by no means continue this most beautiful order. Nor does it escape me that the wise men of this world once held various opinions about providence. Some of them thought that this world was made not by providence but by chance; if their opinion were true, no place would be left for providence, but all things would necessarily drift at random, since the world, which was made by chance, could perish by chance.

Against their false opinion others taught that the world could not have been made without reason, nor certainly continue to exist unless it were ruled by the supreme prudence of its maker. Hence Boethius, a most Christian man, said: O you who govern the world by eternal reason, sower of earth and heaven, who command time to proceed from eternity, and, remaining stable, cause all things to move. And again he said: The generation of all things, and all the progressions of mutable natures, and whatever is moved in any way, derive their causes, order, and forms from the stability of the divine mind.

Others, however, thought that God cared only for incorruptible things, such as the heavenly bodies and separate substances, together with the species of things, but that he knew nothing else at all and utterly neglected all the rest. But these men erred shamefully, because the Almighty has providence and care not only for universal and incorruptible things, but also for particular and corruptible things. Hence the same Boethius again says: But on earth also the lofty founder and ruler of things guides the reins: king and lord, source and origin, law and wise arbiter of equity. He is the continuous love for all things, and the good things seek to be held by their end, because they cannot endure otherwise unless, turned back again by love, they flow back to the causes which he himself gave.

Others, however, unable to bear that they should be neglected, exempted man from the number of corruptible things on account of the preeminence of his intellect, saying that God has care and providence for man, but despises all the other earthly things. Against their false opinion enough, I think, has been said, and to produce many arguments would be altogether superfluous. For Scripture says: You will save men and beasts, O Lord. And in another place a certain wise man said: The small and the great

I iiij. were made by the Lord, and he has care for all alike. Therefore divine majesty's providence orders, rules, disposes, and cares for all lower things, each and every one, great and small, corruptible and incorruptible; his most powerful will produced all things from nothing, as sacred Scripture again bears witness: But your providence, Father, has governed all things from the beginning.

Let men of corrupt mind, impious and reprobate concerning the Christian faith, therefore blush with shame: those who, puffed up with empty talkativeness, take away the providence of him who knows all things, and do not consider what great injury they do to God. For what, to use Firmianus's judgment, is so worthy and so proper to almighty God as providence? But if he foresees nothing, if he neglects lower things, if he does not care for mortal things, he has already lost all his dignity. But it is impossible, as holy Anselm attests, for God to lose his honor, since, as the Peripatetic says, in eternal things there is no evil, nor corruption, nor sin. Therefore whoever takes away providence takes away the whole substance of God. And what does he say except that God does not exist?

But now let those who deny that God's providence cares for lower things tell me: if God neglects lower things, let them consider what necessarily follows. If God knowingly neglects and despises us, there is no longer any cause why we should attend upon him with worship or venerate him with religion, since we obtain no benefit from him; rather, being neglected and despised, let us neglect him ourselves as well.

But if he despises and neglects us unknowingly, there is now no reason at all for us to worship one who does not know us, and on that account is unable to confer any good, or to invoke him with prayers. For if God does not care for human affairs, whether knowingly or unknowingly, every cause for piety ceases, since there is no hope of salvation. What consideration of piety can there be among mortals, what hope for the salvation of souls, if God does not care for human affairs? Indeed, if providence is taken away, whom do we worship, whom do we adore? If there is no providence with God— providence for mortals: certainly he neither grants benefits to human beings nor imposes punishments on deserters; he can neither help mortals, nor wishes to, nor cares at all; he does not notice what we do, and he hears neither the prayers nor the supplications of anyone. Why do we offer him any worship, why honor, why prayers? Or why do we so greatly fear or dread a God who does not know us, who, with us neglected and despised, can neither do us good nor harm?

For once providence is removed, neither holiness nor religion will remain; and when these have been extinguished, the greatest disorder of life and dreadful confusion will follow. Once piety toward God is removed, what will the commonwealth be except everlasting confusion? Public faith among human beings will necessarily perish; the fellowship of the human race and all justice together with it will vanish and perish. What must be thought of the Christian faith if God does not care for human affairs? What, finally, of the Savior of all, our Lord Jesus Christ, except that he will be reckoned an empty fable, wholly fictitious, if there is no providence of God caring for mortal things? Therefore whatever good we do in this life, whatever evil we suffer for the love of God, is wholly vain and useless to us if he has no care for us.

Let those who deny the providence of God now see and shudder, when they perceive that the end of their opinion is the worst despair of all. Therefore let no one, induced by the vain-speaking of secular philosophers, train himself to contempt of God; let no one take away the providence of the highest and unchangeable good; let no one corrupt the dignity of the creator of all things. For all who deny divine providence show themselves both unworthy of the benefits of the most merciful Savior and ungrateful.

For it must be firmly believed, and in no way doubted, that this whole universe, both visible and invisible, and all things individually, whether they are in heaven or on earth or in the sea, are ruled and governed by divine providence, and that absolutely nothing in the whole universe is alien to his care.

I iiij For the fruits of the earth and all the other things that the earth brings forth, and also storms and the various changes of the seasons by which all the things that the earth produces grow naturally to maturity, divine providence supplies for the human race; and it provides for all things individually, not only the great but also the smallest things, to such a degree that not even the thinnest leaf of a tree falls to the ground without the will of almighty God the Father, who created it and rules and cares for it. But if anyone thinks that this vast greatness of the whole universe cannot be ruled and governed by one God, who alone exists, he is greatly deceived, and is shown not to know how great the power of divine might is. Indeed, he who was able to bring the whole universe from nothing into being is also able to govern forever, with the greatest wisdom, what he has made. For he knows all things, understands all things, and can do all things, he who alone, omnipotent, created all things.

Therefore we, believing the holy Gospel, should above all venerate divine providence; we should also raise our minds upward, with what strength we can, away from the things that are transitory, and, brought back to ourselves, be united, so that we may faithfully understand the majesty of God present everywhere. Since it is wholly uncircumscribable, it holds all things, fills all things, embraces all things, surpasses all things, and sustains all things. It does not sustain from one side and surpass from another, nor fill from one side and encompass from another; rather, by encompassing it fills, by filling it super-encompasses, by sustaining it surpasses, and by surpassing it sustains all things. By the mass of a body he is nowhere, and by his uncircumscribable substance he is nowhere absent; he is not seen by the eyes of flesh, but is seen through faith in purity of heart. O inexplicable power, O incomprehensible goodness, O ineffable wisdom, O uncircumscribable divinity, which does not consist of parts like a body, nor of passions.

...you are not divided as a soul is; you do not underlie forms as do all the other things that have been made through you; you are in all things and above all things, ruling and governing the universe with the greatest wisdom. By these testimonies, therefore, most sacred Caesar Maximilian, it has been sufficiently proved, as I think, that this whole universe is governed by the providence of God. Since he is pure intellect, simple, uncreated, and eternal, he knows all things, understands all things, foreknows all things; and since he is almighty by nature, he can do all things. To him nothing is difficult, nothing impossible; he created such wondrous things by his power; he established them in truth; by reason he perfected them; by strength he sustains them; by goodness he illumines them. To him be praise, to him honor, to him glory, who lives and reigns, God glorious and exalted, forever and ever. Amen.

THE AUTHOR'S DECLARATION TO CAESAR.

These, most unconquered Caesar Maximilian, are the things that seemed to me should be said in reply to the Eight Questions proposed by your majesty. For you wished to have my judgment on them also in writing, making an estimate of me beyond the truth, since I am not to be compared in talent with those whose opinion you heard before me. Let pardon make me worthy if I have said anything less proper; for, at the command of your highness, set as a traveler on a journey, I dictated as I could, at intervals, whatever occurred to me to answer. But I say from my mind and openly declare that I am a sincere confessor of the Christian faith, and that I wish to remain until death in the union of the sacrosanct Roman Church. Therefore, if anything either in this lucubration of mine or in others should be found said or written otherwise than that Church holds, thinks, believes, and teaches, as a true son of obedience, by the attestation of these presents I now simply revoke it, and wish it to be and to be held perpetually revoked.

Wherefore, most wise Caesar, I both humbly ask and earnestly admonish your majesty that, before you cause my responses to come to the knowledge of those for whom they are destined and kept, you have them approved by the judgment of many. For great care must be taken that nothing be proposed to those for whose salvation your serenity keeps watch except what is solid, approved, manifest, and lawfully confirmed in the Catholic faith by the opinion of very many wise men. May almighty God by his providence direct and guard you always to the praise of his name, Maximilian, greatest of emperors. From the city of Neometana, on the tenth day of the month of July, in the year of Christians one thousand five hundred and eight.

Printed at Oppenheim at the expense of Johannes Hasselberg, of Augia in the diocese of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1515, on the twentieth day of the month of September.
